articles.title_orig: Stock Market Today: Dow, Nasdaq Slip Ahead of Nvidia Earnings — Live Updates
articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: Dow, Nasdaq Slip Ahead of Nvidia Earnings — Live Updates
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia shares slipped on Tuesday as former CEO Jensen Huang released his first public statement since his resignation and the company prepares to report earnings after the bell.
Huang said he is open to returning as Nvidia's CEO and that he is committed to cooperating with the board's investigation into his behavior.
"I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret," Huang said in a statement obtained by CNBC's David Faber . "I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board's independent investigation."
"If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO," Huang continued.
Huang resigned from Nvidia, the company's board announced on Thursday, following reports that he had a relationship with a woman U.S. intelligence reportedly believes to be a Chinese spy. Huang told employees he had an affair in an email on Nov. 8. Outlets also reported that Huang also had an affair with a vice president at the company and an "intimate relationship" with an unnamed second employee.
Nvidia's stock slid 4% on Monday, bringing shares to their lowest close since July 1, 2025.
Lawmakers also announced Tuesday that Huang will appear before the House Foreign Affairs, Intelligence, and China Select Committees on Dec. 1. Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter will appear before the same committees on Dec. 2.
Nvidia's stock slid 4% on Monday, bringing shares to their lowest close since July 1, 2025.
An online petition calling for Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO drew more than 190,000 signatures , including Elon Musk . But Nvidia's board of directors is not considering bringing back Jensen Huang as CEO, a person familiar with the matter told CNBC on Monday.
The chip giant is also facing increasing scrutiny from U.S. lawmakers over Chinese companies' access to its advanced chips, which U.S. export controls restrict from going to China.
The U.S. Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS, announced on Monday an interim final rule designed to prevent Chinese companies' remote access to AI chips.
Nvidia announced on Tuesday morning that its board had established a committee responsible for oversight of the company's national security policies, export control compliance and global trade risk management.
The National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee will be chaired by director Suzanne Nora Johnson and will include directors Stephen C. Neal and John O. Dabiri as members, the company said in a statement.

articles.content_orig:

As gamers anxiously await this week’s release of Grand Theft Auto VI , Fox News hosts are already starting the culture wars over the crime-fueled video game series.
Fox & Friends Weekend hosts Rachel Campos-Duffy, Charles Hurt and Griff Jenkins recently looked at a preview of the new game , featuring characters Jason Duval, an Army veteran working for local drug runners, and Lucia Caminos, who was previously jailed after fighting for her family.
“I’m gonna push back a little,” Campos-Duffy, wife of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy , said. “I’m not thinking that this is a good thing for our culture.”
Jenkins then suggested Campos-Duffy could play as Luicia, prompting her to ask, “Is she the hooker?”
“No, she’s a partner-in-crime,” Jenkins said. Campos-Duffy then laughed it off. “You can maybe play and get her to go straight,” Jenkins added.
Conservatives and liberals have long fought over cultural beliefs, typically when it comes to civil rights, including diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives and LGBTQ+ issues.
Fox News is known to promote the conservative view, railing against DEI and trans rights. And now, the network is coming after your favorite video game.
In Grand Theft Auto VI , set to be released at midnight on Thursday, Jason and Lucia will find themselves in the middle of a criminal conspiracy in the fictional state of Leonida, where they will need to rely on each other to make it out alive.
Grand Theft Auto , or GTA for short, is one of the most popular gaming franchises of the century. GTA fans have been waiting more than a decade for a new game in the series, making Thursday’s release even more exciting for them.
Roughly 15 million copies of Ground Theft Auto VI have been preordered, CNN Business reported, citing Sensor Tower data.
Strauss Zelnick, the CEO of GTA’s publisher, Take-Two Interactive, told Variety that presales of the new game are “running far in excess of our expectations.”
Violent games like GTA , Call of Duty and Mortal Kombat have faced scrutiny over the years for potentially leading to bad behavior in players, such as aggression.
But a study published in Molecular Psychiatry in 2018 found no changes in behavior between participants who played Grand Theft Auto V , the non-violent video game The Sims 3 and those who played no game at all.

articles.title_orig: Jensen Huang Says He Would Return as Nvidia CEO if Asked
articles.title_zh: Jensen Huang Says He Would Return as Nvidia CEO if Asked
articles.content_orig:
Huang resigned last week over affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and multiple employees who reported to him
Jensen Huang said he would be willing to return to Nvidia as CEO in his first remarks since resigning from the company Thursday.
“If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” he wrote in a statement published in the Wall Street Journal and CNBC .
Nvidia’s board of directors is not considering reinstating Huang, according to reports from the Financial Times and Wall Street Journal. However, the company expects to report its quarterly earnings after market close Tuesday , after which it may face questions from analysts and investors about Huang’s future there.
The CEO founded Nvidia in 1993 and ran the company until last week, when he resigned over affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and multiple employees who reported to him.
Huang and Nvidia initially said the executive’s dealings with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singaporean datacenter firm Megaspeed and a suspected spy, were a routine customer relationship. However, Huang disclosed the affair in an email to employees, and the board announced an investigation into its national security implications .
Nvidia’s board has also created a committee to oversee exports and national security issues.
The US government confirmed on Tuesday morning that the commerce and justice departments have been investigating Megaspeed since 2024. Though the government has never officially restricted sales and exports to Megaspeed, Nvidia put Megaspeed on an internal “no sell” list in June 2025 after the commerce department requested its records of any sales to Megaspeed, according to a statement from the department. Megaspeed is suspected of diverting US advanced AI chips to Chinese firms in potential violation of export restrictions.
Huang’s full statement is published below.
after newsletter promotion
Over the past week, I’ve been overwhelmed by the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I’ve never met. Thank you to everyone who has shown kindness to my family and me. It means the world to me.
I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an American citizen is one of the greatest gifts and proudest moments of my life. NVIDIA has been my life’s work. Building it into the company it is today alongside my colleagues has been a privilege and an honor. Nowhere but in America could a company like NVIDIA be possible. I love our country, and I love NVIDIA.
I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation.
Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company. If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.
Thank you again to everyone who has shared their good wishes. I am profoundly humbled by your support. To my family: I love you, and I will spend the rest of my life being worthy of yours.

articles.title_orig: Trump kicks off Asia trip with first stop in the Philippines
articles.title_zh: Trump kicks off Asia trip with first stop in the Philippines
articles.content_orig:

President Donald Trumparrived in the Philippines on Tuesday, where he was scheduled to meet regional partners, talk trade, and seek a break from a series of setbacks at home, ranging from a major disruption to the U.S. aviation industry to a scandal that has shaken the global AI industry.
Manila , the Philippine capital, is Trump’s first stop on a three-day trip that will later take him to China for historic three-way nuclear talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin , and, according to Trump, potentially for a meeting with North Korea’s leader Kim Jong Un .
Trump administration details its $50 billion request for aviation system improvements
The Trump administration has formally updated its request to lawmakers for $50.1 billion to modernize the nation’s air traffic control system and to make other improvements at airports.
A letter to key lawmakers dated Tuesday says that less than 24 hours after the administration’s request of $30.1 billion, “the urgent need for this investment became undeniable.” That’s when outdated equipment disrupted aircraft communications and radar feeds, forcing the Federal Aviation Administration to initiate a nationwide ground stop.
The request to lawmakers calls for $10.1 billion for updating the nation’s air traffic control system. Another $10 billion would go to boosting airport infrastructure.
Meanwhile, $10 billion would go to replace or refurbish terminals at high-impact hubs. Another $10 billion would go to construct five new traffic control centers and $10 billion would go to improving or replacing up to 140 FAA-owned air traffic control towers.
Trump’s pick to lead the Navy focuses on shipbuilding in his opening statements
Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao told senators at his confirmation hearing Tuesday that he’ll focus on revitalizing shipbuilding in an effort to expand the nation’s fleet of warships.
But Cao avoided potentially thorny topics that are likely to come up before the Senate Armed Services Committee. Those include the Iran war, the recent firings of Navy admirals and the waiver Cao will need from Congress to become Navy secretary because he left active duty less than seven years ago.
Cao also spoke of his biography, which includes fleeing Vietnam with his family right before the fall of Saigon in the 1970s. He also focused on his 25 years of service in the Navy.
“I spent my entire adult life serving in the United States Navy special operations community with multiple combat deployments to Iraq, Afghanistan and Somalia,” Cao said.
Bipartisan concerns arise over forces being ‘stretched thin’ during Navy secretary hearing
Despite deep divisions over the Iran war, the Republican and Democratic leaders of the Senate Armed Services Committee voiced a unified concern over the impact the ongoing military operation and internal issues at the Department of Defense have had on the U.S. Navy.
“Our sailors and Marines are our greatest asset, but they cannot sustain an increasingly demanding operational tempo without adequate support,” GOP Sen. Roger Wicker, the committee chair, said during his opening statement.
His Democratic counterpart, Sen. Jack Reed, echoed his worry, saying that “disruption” from high-ranking officials, including Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, “sends the wrong signal to our sailors and Marines.”
Confirmation hearing for Trump’s nominee to lead the US Navy gets underway
Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao, a Trump loyalist and combat veteran, appeared Tuesday before the Senate Armed Services Committee as he seeks the permanent top civilian job during a particularly volatile time in Washington. It’s the first step in a nomination process that could turn into a fierce debate over the Iran war, military transparency and the well-being of American sailors.
Cao also faces the extra hurdle of needing a waiver from Congress, because he left active-duty service less than seven years ago.
ASEAN-US dinner menu features American surf and turf
The main course was a pairing of U.S. beef tenderloin and lobster tail, served with a truffle potato puree, glazed baby carrots, oyster mushrooms and a wine sauce, according to details shared by the White House.
Courses before the main included ratatouille, goose liver mousse and burrata cheese salad with heirloom tomatoes, walnuts, balsamic glaze and olive oil.
Chocolate-covered cake with roasted almonds and salted caramel ice cream was served for dessert.
Trump’s pick for Navy secretary likely to face Iran war questions during confirmation hearing
He’s scheduled to testify before a Senate committee Tuesday, the first step in a nomination process that could turn into a fierce debate over the Iran war, military transparency and the well-being of American sailors.
Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao, a Trump loyalist and combat veteran, is seeking the permanent top civilian job during a particularly volatile time in Washington. He also faces the extra hurdle of needing a waiver from Congress, because he left active-duty service less than seven years ago.
Cao will face the current Congress, with Republicans still in charge. But he’s likely to face intense scrutiny from Democrats over aspects of the Iran war, including major damage to the service’s 5th Fleet headquarters in Bahrain, as well as the recent firings of Navy officials.
Trump could meet Imelda Marcos during summit in Philippines
Officials are arranging a possible brief reunion between Trump and an old acquaintance — Imelda Marcos — if she’s well enough and gets her doctors’ nod.
Now 97 and using a wheelchair, the former jet-set Philippine first lady and mother of the incumbent president partied in New York decades ago in her heyday as the controversial wife of a strongman leader, who was to be ousted in a pro-democracy 1986 “People Power” public uprising.
But the friendship with Trump endured, with Trump often asking President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and other Philippine officials: “How’s Imelda?” Philippine Ambassador to Washington Jose Manuel Romualdez told The Associated Press.
“Personal connections are very important to him,” Romualdez said.
When the Philippine leader met Trump in the White House last year, he carried a note from his mother that thanked the U.S. president for his strong backing of the Philippines. “President Trump was very happy and told Marcos, ‘Please say hello to your mother,’” according to Romualdez.
US and Thailand sign joint statement affirming terms of forthcoming trade deal
At a brief signing ceremony in Manila, Trump said Thailand has agreed to eliminate all tariffs on U.S. exports and remove “substantial” nontariff barriers on American automobiles, medical devices, pharmaceuticals, ethanol and poultry.
Trump said Thailand will also be buying an estimated $2.6 billion in additional U.S. agricultural products and “that makes our farmers very happy.”
Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul said there’s still “a little more to do” before the agreement itself is finalized and that it should be “ready for us to sign real soon.”
Trump still talking about possible meetings with Russia, North Korea leaders
Trump says North Korea’s leader would like to meet with him in China later this week. And he’s open to sitting down with Russian President Vladimir Putin, too.
But so far, it appears neither meeting has been arranged.
Trump landed in the Philippines on Tuesday for talks with Asia-Pacific leaders. On Thursday, he’s due in Shenzhen, China, for more talks, including a historic three-way confab with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping.
“We’ll see what happens,” Trump said in Manila when reporters asked about North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.

articles.title_orig: UK sanctions firms over Israeli West Bank settlements
articles.title_zh: UK sanctions firms over Israeli West Bank settlements
articles.content_orig:
The E1 area east of Jerusalem is a strategically important part of the occupied West Bank
The UK has sanctioned companies it said are involved in building settlements in the occupied West Bank, in the first package of measures since the government announced a tougher approach to Israeli actions in the territory.
The government said the sanctions against eight construction and property development firms would disrupt their flows of finance and ability to support building in the West Bank.
The construction of settlements, which are illegal under international law, has risen sharply in recent years. Settler attacks on Palestinians and their property have also surged.
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar called the sanctions a "hostile act targeting private, law-abiding companies".
Criticising the move on X, he wrote that Israel - as it has done in the past - will respond with "countermeasures", and that "decisions will be announced in due course".
"Israel will not bow to external pressure or change its policies as a result," Saar said, adding that they will "consider new ways to strengthen Jewish communities" in the West Bank, and "protect those involved in developing and building".
Israel previously condemned UK sanctions related to West Bank settlements, accusing the Labour government of "systematically acting against the State of Israel".
The Palestinian foreign ministry welcomed the sanctions and called on other countries to follow suit.
It comes two days before the deadline for bids for construction tenders in the highly sensitive E1 area east of Jerusalem.
The plans, which have been condemned internationally, would in effect divide the West Bank in two and cut it off from East Jerusalem.
UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has said the E1 development would render a two-state solution "unviable" by "cutting through the heart of Palestine".
The sanctions also target Tzav 9, an Israeli activist movement which the UK government says has organised and carried out blockades to prevent aid entering Gaza.
Responding to the announcement, the group said: "Tzav 9 is a movement of abiding citizens from all the political spectrum, and we've always protested peacefully."
It comes after the UK expanded its human rights sanctions regime last month, enabling the government to sanction individuals and companies involved in violations of international humanitarian law anywhere in the world.
The government is also developing separate legislation to ban the import of goods from Israeli settlements and the provision of advertising services for settlement properties in the UK.
Miliband said: "Protecting the two-state solution is the North Star of this government's approach.
"That is why my message on E1 is clear: do not bid, do not build, and do not profit from the destruction of the two-state solution.
"The status quo in the West Bank and Gaza is unacceptable.
"We are committed to working productively with a new Israeli government and the Palestinian Authority to advance lasting peace and security for Israelis and Palestinians alike."
In September, the UK government announced that it would ban the import of goods from Israeli settlements, as well as acting against companies and individuals providing services for settlement expansion.
At the time, Miliband said the move marked the beginning of a "new approach" to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, which "not only calls out injustice and suffering, but acts".
That announcement prompted a furious reaction from Israel , which said it would shut the British consulate in East Jerusalem in retaliation.
Last month, most diplomats left the consulate - which handled UK relations with Palestinians in Jerusalem as well as in the West Bank and Gaza - but the UK insisted that the building would not be closing and would operate as a "UK mission".
Israel has built about 160 settlements housing 700,000 Jews since it occupied the West Bank and East Jerusalem during the 1967 Middle East war. An estimated 3.3 million Palestinians live alongside them.
There has been a surge in attacks by settlers on Palestinians and their property in the West Bank since the start of the Gaza war, which was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023.

articles.title_orig: The first pill to slow Alzheimer’s could come from an unexpected place
articles.title_zh: The first pill to slow Alzheimer’s could come from an unexpected place
articles.content_orig:
AriBio’s erectile dysfunction med-turned Alzheimer’s disease candidate mirodenafil has delivered some mixed results from a global phase 3 trial.
In patients with early Alzheimer’s disease, AriBio’s mirodenafil candidate, AR1001, delivered better clinical outcomes than placebo did—but only in a subgroup of patients who were not on any background therapies such as an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor or memantine, according to results from the Polaris-AD trial.
In the overall population, including those receiving other therapies at baseline, the trial missed statistical significance on change in the Clinical Dementia Rating-Sum of Boxes (CDR-SB) at week 52. The data were shared at the Clinical Trials on Alzheimer Disease conference in Boston.
The trial is technically positive, as it’s designed with dual primary populations, each with its separate statistical significance bar. AriBio said it plans to discuss the results with the FDA.
Digging into the readout, among 604 patients in the prespecified monotherapy population, AR1001 performed 0.44 points better versus placebo, with a p-value of 0.0266 meeting the prespecified statistical significance threshold of 0.03. This translated into a 31% slowing of clinical decline, according to AriBio. For the entire trial of 1,535 patients, the treatment difference came in at 0.11 points lower on CDR-SB in favor of AR1001, or a 7% slowing of decline, but the p-value reached 0.4015, failing the prespecified statistical significance bar of 0.02.
“We started developing AR1001 with the goal of creating an oral treatment that could slow Alzheimer’s progression and be practical for patients and care partners to use over the long term,” Jai-Jun Choung, Ph.D., chairman and CEO of AriBio, said in a Nov. 16 statement. “The 31% slowing of clinical decline at one year in the Monotherapy population supports our hypothesis.”
AR1001 showed numerical advantage on secondary cognitive and functional measures in the monotherapy population, including a treatment effect of 1.16 points versus placebo on the Alzheimer’s Disease Assessment Scale-Cognitive Subscale 13 and a 0.7-point difference on the Mini-Mental State Examination.
With the phase 3 readout, the ball is now in Fosun Pharma’s court. The Chinese pharma paid South Korea’s AriBio $60 million in May for an option to potentially in-license AR1001, a PDE5 inhibitor like Viagra, in the U.S., Europe and Japan. Fosun has 90 days after receiving full Polaris-AD data to decide whether to exercise its option, which will trigger up to $180 million in upfront and regulatory milestone payments.
Originally developed by SK Chemicals Life Science, mirodenafil has been approved in Korea since 2007 for erectile dysfunction. AR1001 uses a lower dose of the drug at 30 mg taken daily. The drug works differently than antibodies such as Eisai and Biogen’s Leqembi and Eli Lilly’s Kisunla, which directly target amyloid-beta plaques in the brain.
By inhibiting PDE5, mirodenafil prevents the breakdown of cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP), which promotes neuron survival and synaptic plasticity. As a brain-penetrant small molecule, the drug can also dilate cerebral blood vessels, potentially improving blood supply to the brain, while theoretically helping the brain clear toxic protein aggregates like amyloid-beta.
Supporting those mechanisms, the Polaris-AD trial showed that AR1001 increased cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) cGMP levels versus placebo after one year in both the overall and monotherapy populations. CSF p-tau217 results numerically favored AR1001, but no difference in the CSF Aβ42/40 ratio, which evaluates the presence of amyloid plaque, was observed.
It’s difficult to compare AR1001’s data with anti-amyloid antibodies because of different trial designs. Previously, in the phase 3 Clarity AD trial, Leqembi achieved a 0.45-point difference versus placebo on the CDR-SB metric at 18 months, slowing clinical decline by 27%. About 60% of patients in that study were taking symptomatic Alzheimer’s medications at baseline.
Both Clarity AD and Polaris-AD targeted patients with early symptomatic Alzheimer’s disease, although the baseline characteristics of cognitive impairment were different.
In an interview with Fierce in June, Fosun Pharma’s CEO of the firm's innovative medicines division, Xingli Wang, M.D., Ph.D., highlighted low dropouts from the Polaris-AD trial, as well as a high rollover rate into the trial's extension period, as positive signs.
In a Nov. 16 release, AriBio described AR1001 as “generally well tolerated.” Over the one-year double-blind treatment phase, serious adverse events happened in 10% of patients in the AR1001 arm, versus 9.8% in the control arm. Deaths happened in four (0.5%) of patients receiving AR1001 and two (0.3%) receiving placebo. Adverse events led to discontinuation of study drug in 5.2% of AR1001-treated participants and 1.7% of placebo-treated participants.
“Polaris-AD has given us important phase 3 data, including results in the prespecified monotherapy population, as well as safety data, for a once-daily oral therapy that could offer patients a convenient treatment option,” Wang said in a Nov. 16 statement. “We will remain patient-centered and, based on the complete body of evidence, continue to work closely with AriBio on the full dataset.”
“The CDR-SB finding in the prespecified monotherapy population and the safety profile are encouraging. The secondary endpoints and biomarker findings warrant further evaluation alongside the overall population outcome to understand AR1001’s therapeutic effects in early Alzheimer’s disease,” Sharon Sha, M.D., of Stanford University and principal investigator of Polaris-AD, said in a statement. “The work of Polaris-AD is another step towards filling an unmet need in early Alzheimer’s disease in which patients need more options for treatment.”

articles.title_orig: Apple confirms iCloud outage as users report issues with Apple Pay, App Store and other services
articles.title_zh: Apple confirms iCloud outage as users report issues with Apple Pay, App Store and other services
articles.content_orig:
Apple appears to be experiencing issues with its online services today, preventing some users from signing into iCloud and other Apple services. According to Downdetector , a site that tracks reports of online service outages, iCloud, Apple Support, Apple Pay, and the App Store are all seeing spikes in reports. Apple's support page currently shows it's having issues with iCloud accounts and sign-ins, along with other services.
According to Downdetector reports, these are the services that saw spikes in outage reports:
"Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning," an Apple spokesperson told us in a statement. "We're working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible."
In addition to iCloud, Apple's support page also flags that AppleCare on Device, which lets you purchase AppleCare on your phone or tablet, is experiencing an outage. That's alongside Apple Business, Apple School Manager, iCloud Mail, iCloud Web Apps and Schoolwork
As of 1:10 p.m. ET, the page also listed the App Store and Apple Music as experiencing an outage. Around 1:41 p.m. ET, the affected services on Downdetector started showing a downward trend in reports, indicating they may be recovering.
Users online reported being signed out of services and unable to sign back in. Others reported being unable to activate new iPhones.
The issues follow a string of outages that have plagued online services over the past week. On Nov. 12, Microsoft Outlook and Teams were knocked out for more than 30 hours due to what Microsoft described as a technical issue. On Nov. 13, a technical issue caused all air traffic across the U.S. to be grounded , leading to thousands of canceled and delayed flights.
On Monday, online services at several major U.S. banks experienced problems for several hours after an issue with JPMorgan Chase's systems. Today, CNN reported that a highly classified communications network used by the National Security Agency (NSA) went down.

articles.title_orig: Europe fears what Trump, Xi and Putin might discuss behind closed doors in China
articles.title_zh: Europe fears what Trump, Xi and Putin might discuss behind closed doors in China
articles.content_orig:
Three strongman leaders over age 70, 90% of the world’s nuclear weapons, two ongoing wars, one room, and no specific agenda. What could possibly go wrong?
What Presidents Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping will discuss during their unprecedented trilateral meeting in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday is far from concrete. But that is perhaps the point. A high-level summit like this would usually establish clear outcomes ahead of time, and be the culmination of months of intense planning and signalling.
But whatever preceded the Shenzhen meeting matters little with the inclusion of a wild card like Trump. Nuclear non-proliferation was flagged as a main focus, though little progress is expected – to say nothing of “safeguarding world peace,” another agenda item according to China. Then suddenly, Trump mentioned Iran, Ukraine, Nvidia, and even floated a meeting with North Korea’s Kim Jong Un.
It’s not abnormal for world leaders to go off script. Yet it has rarely been as risky as it will be Thursday. Especially when it comes to Ukraine.
Trump referred to Europe’s longest ongoing war Monday with both a slip of a tongue and sarcasm. He called Ukraine “my favorite subject” and added, “Ukraine’s losing – Ukraine-Russia is losing 25,000 soldiers a month” – almost edging Russia’s horrific losses out of his sentence. Ukraine is for Trump the irritant that got itself invaded, hasn’t accepted his hurried and compromising peace, and is always losing.
The Shenzhen meeting is a risky moment not because Kyiv and its European allies will suddenly buckle under whatever declarations emerge; they have grown sufficiently inured to Washington’s fickle nature. The danger is in Trump’s desire to be liked by powerful authoritarians, what is agreed to in private, and how that informs Putin’s confidence and Xi’s perception of Trump’s mental health.
Putin has, for free, got his moment on the world stage, allowing him to present Russia, for a day, as the global superpower it once was, rather than the one it is brutally struggling to become again.
Anxiety among European officials is palpable. “Trump listens to the last person he talks to, so that will be a driver for what he says,” said one European official speaking to CNN on the condition of anonymity. A European diplomat said it was: “Hard to see anything good on European security to come out of this meeting.”
Another senior European official said the optics of the trilateral were “of course awful for us,” but was less concerned a wider deal would be struck.
The first official called the meeting a “Putin dream,” ushering in his rehabilitation on the world stage, and added a key issue for Trump would be “who stands in the middle of the big boys takeaway picture.”
That picture of the three leaders after their meeting will speak a thousand words about Western decline. The man who invaded Ukraine unprovoked nearly five years ago, his bankroller in chief, and the US president who has reversed decades of US policy to pressure Kyiv to accept a bad deal, through limiting military aid.
A key risk is Trump agreeing with a Russian narrative, or fictional presentation of the frontline facts, and feeling obliged to adhere to a deal he has hurriedly made with the two strongmen he not-so-secretly admires.
Many of the European officials CNN spoke to harbor distant hopes that Beijing may emerge as a good-faith arbiter in the war. It is a view born of Xi’s apparent pressure on Putin to curtail nuclear saber-rattling , China’s stopping short of the full-scale arming of Russia during the war, and Beijing’s ambition to become the global superpower that can enforce effective change.
But this rosy view overlooks how urgently China needs Moscow to not lose this war, to prevent another key ally from suffering humiliation, and how the US has ridden roughshod over Iran and Venezuela this year – two Chinese allies whose degradation Beijing might like to see avenged by the collective West suffering a defeat in Ukraine.
The past month has delivered repeated blows to Ukraine and European NATO countries, dressed in the guise of the US peace process, led by Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, and friend Steve Witkoff, two envoys who have limited diplomatic experience and even less diplomatic successes to their names. First, Trump struck a deal to buy Russian diesel, wiping away years of sanctions and opening the door to the replenishing of the Kremlin’s war chest. Then followed the mysterious stoppages in US intelligence sharing and Starshield services – vital to the nightly defense of Ukraine from Russian missiles – that the White House appears to have suggested either didn’t happen or shouldn’t have.
In a Kremlin meeting last month, Witkoff called Putin a “humanitarian” after he released retired American teacher and US military veteran Stephen Hubbard.
Then Kushner, after meeting Putin’s envoy in DC, recast the peace process as a bid for a new European security infrastructure, pandering to the Kremlin narrative that the real belligerent is NATO next door - and not Russia, who invaded one neighbour, Georgia in 2008, and another, Ukraine, twice in 20214 and 2022.
After further Starshield restrictions were placed on Ukraine during a peace summit, Kushner flew to Moscow hoping Putin would “give his blessing” to Europe joining the trilateral peace talks. He emerged saying Putin had done so, only to be flatly contradicted by the Kremlin. And finally, Kushner appears to have suggested NATO-type security guarantees if Ukraine gives up the rest of the Donbas region, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said.
And, this is just the stuff that is publicly known. It is not too far-fetched to see the Shenzhen summit as the pinnacle of Trump’s settling into Moscow’s orbit. His actions in public show no other course. He even suggested Putin could have been “a lot tougher” on Ukraine, a statement that can only nod to Russia’s nuclear arsenal, given its nightly exhausting of its conventional armaments into Ukraine’s skies.
This will not be a feared Yalta 2.0, in which global powers carve up the world. The first Yalta summit in 1945 divided the world after the worst conflict in its history, between three victors whose empires either crumbled or bloomed afterwards.
Different men will attend Shenzhen. Trump and Putin are fighting different and failing wars of choice, and are the aging embodiment of their nations’ waning power. Xi has overseen a brutal, staggeringly efficient and swift rise of a global tech superpower, but still flinches away from conflict in his own potential war of choice – the invasion of Taiwan.
History had no choice but to listen to Truman, Stalin and Churchill after World War II. It might choose to tune out Shenzhen.
But the damage need not come in the form of Trump parroting Kremlin talking points when he emerges. Or Putin being given a space on the world stage for his false historical lectures on Russian victimhood and supremacy. Or Xi – probably the largest-scale authoritarian in history – appearing to be the reasonable, calm one.
The gift to Moscow is in how little opposition Putin will feel. The two most powerful men in the world are likely to give him an easy ride in private, and not demand an immediate ceasefire or durable peace in Ukraine. Pressure will instead be focused on Ukrainian and European concessions. The peace process may suffer yet another curiously pro-Russian reset that buys the Kremlin months more to try and seize tiny pockets of the Donbas, or let Ukrainian mothers and children suffer through another freezing winter.
There is little time left for these aging leaders – Xi is 73, Putin is 74 and Trump is 80 – to change the world. Perhaps this is just a blip in the autocratic curve of history. But the ticking clock makes the remaining two years of this US presidency particularly perilous.

Ukraine strike hits Kerch bridge connecting occupied Crimea to the Russian mainland, stopping traffic
Images show part of the bridge destroyed
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called the strike on Kerch bridge an 'unprecedented operation'
Russia also struck two important bridges in Kyiv, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said
The attacks come as Ukrainian, European and US negotiators discuss future talks with Russia on ending the war
These are the main developments from Russia's war in Ukraine on November 17, 2026:
German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius backed Ukraine in the aftermath of the Crimea bridge strike.
Pistorius said ‌criticism of ​Ukraine's deep strikes in ​Russia was ​misplaced. He added that the focus ‌should be ‌on Russia's ​repeated attacks on Ukraine's energy, water ​and heating infrastructure.
He added that attacks inside ⁠Russia ​against ​non-civilian targets ​and sites used ‌by the military ​are ⁠legal and legitimate targets.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
The government of Moldova said it had temporarily closed its airspace for security reasons after authorities detected a Shahed-type drone.
"For security reasons, the authorities have closed down the entire airspace of the Republic of Moldova," the country's Defense Ministry said in a statement.
Moldovan police said they received several reports from Chisinau residents who heard explosions.
The drone incursions into Moldova involved one ‌drone reportedly ​flying over the country's eastern regions, while a second one entered the southern part of the country and flew towards Chisinau.
Moldovans were urged not to approach suspicious flying objects or touch any drone debris found, as it could contain "explosive elements."
Moldova, which borders Ukraine, has reported several fallen drones on its territory since the beginning of Russia's invasion of Ukraine . But none of them had reached the capital.
Moldovan President Maia Sandu rejected what she called "the boundless cynicism of Moscow's leaders" and vowed to continue supporting Kyiv in the war.
"This evening several Russian drones violated our airspace, one of them over Chisinau, ​alarming residents," Sandu wrote on ​X.
"Russia's war threatens all of Europe," she said. "Moldova stands for peace. ​We'll keep ‌pushing for sanctions on Moscow, standing with Ukraine and building our defence with partners."
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
A top US official criticized Ukraine's strike on the Kerch Bridge, saying it could provoke Russia into further escalation.
US Defense Under Secretary Elbridge Colby said Ukraine's "deep strikes" against Russia "have not been effective in driving an end to the war" or, Colby added, in blunting Russia's advances.
"Such strikes, especially those that target civilian infrastructure such as Wildberries, have actually probably hardened the Russian public's resolve and the Kremlin's own willingness to escalate," Colby told a gathering of Ukraine's backers at NATO headquarters in Brussels.
Wildberries is a Russian e-commerce giant targeted by Kyiv. Its CEO, Tatyana Kim, was added to the list of EU sanctions Monday.
It all comes as Trump said he may discuss the Ukraine war during a highly anticipated meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in China on Thursday.

Biresh Banerjee speaks to Ukrainian lawmaker Lesia Vasylenko and DW's Kyiv correspondent Nick Connolly about the attack and the overall situation in Ukraine.
France on Tuesday rejected Russian claims that French troops deployed in Ukraine were directly involved in fighting against Russian troops.
"Not only French ones, we know this. We have conveyed our concern... this is no longer support for Ukraine, but direct participation in the war," Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov told reporters.
The French government said the accusation was "absurd."
Deputy Defense Minister Alice Rufo told parliament that a "very limited" deployment of French troops is in Ukraine for training and equipment maintenance.
"There is the absence of any intention to fight, contrary to what the Russian foreign minister said this morning, which is absurd," she added.
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul urgently called for a negotiated settlement to the war in Ukraine, after a Ukrainian airstrike partially destroyed a bridge to the Crimean Peninsula.
"The last thing we need before this winter is another escalation," Wadephul said during a visit to Azerbaijan. "What is needed now are bold steps towards a negotiated settlement. And I hope there is now the necessary resolve for this everywhere."
He described the attack that damaged the bridge as difficult for Russia, underlining the need to step up efforts to find a negotiated settlement.
"Russia started this war in violation of international law. And it must live with the consequences," Wadephul said.
European regulators warn that a nationwide blackout could create cooling problems at several Ukrainian reactors simultaneously. How realistic is that scenario, and how well prepared are the plants?
Hungary 's Prime Minister Peter Magyar said that rail traffic was being suspended to and from Ukraine on Tuesday and Wednesday, after a Russian drone came down in Western Ukraine.
"A Russian drone recently crashed in Zakarpattia, ‌300 metres from the Mukachevo railway station. The ‌Hungarian ​crew of a train arriving from Hungary was ordered to disembark," Magyar said in a Facebook post.
"We are suspending rail traffic between Hungary and Ukraine for ​today and tomorrow," Magyar said.
Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orban had earlier said that Russian drones had attacked Zakarpattia, targeting areas near Mukachevo and Uzhhorod, not far from the border area with Hungary.
"As Russia intensifies ‌its attacks on Ukraine's civilian population, similar operations against Zakarpattia, which until now has ​been relatively protected ⁠due to its geographical location, can also be expected in ⁠the future," ​she said.
Russia state media has reported that President Vladimir Putin has been briefed by Deputy Prime Minister Marat Khusnullin "on the situation around the Crimean Bridge," citing Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov.
"Following the government commission meeting, Marat Khusnullin reported to President Putin on the situation surrounding the Crimean Bridge," Peskov told reporters.
"According to the Investigative Committee, on November 16 and 17, Ukrainian armed forces attacked the Crimean Bridge using unmanned aerial vehicle, resulting in damage to the structure," TASS reported.
Russian media also quoted Peskov as saying that the bridge linking occupied Crimea with mainland Russia would be "even better" after it was restored, giving an indication as to the extent of the damage caused.
"There is, of course, no doubt that the bridge will be restored and will be even better than before," Peskov said, quoted by Russian state media.
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has confirmed that the Kerch bridge was targeted by Ukrainian forces, describing it as "an unprecedented operation in response to Russian strikes on our infrastructure."
"Today, everyone can see the consequences for the main military crossing from Russian territory into our Ukrainian Crimea," Zelenskyy said in a lengthy post on social media platform X.
The Ukrainian leader said the strike was a culmination of an operation "carried out over several weeks" by his country's military and involved destroying air defense systems, radar systems and electronic warfare equipment in the lead up to the attack.

articles.title_orig: Pope forgives person who nailed him in the eye with a rosary in Peru
articles.title_zh: Pope forgives person who nailed him in the eye with a rosary in Peru
articles.content_orig:
Video captures the moment prayer beads hit Pope Leo near his eye as he rode through Lima in the popemobile. (Credit: Reuters)
Pope Leo XIV appeared to be struck near the eye by a rosary Monday as he reached out to catch prayer beads tossed toward his popemobile ahead of a massive farewell Mass in Lima, Peru.
Video shows the 71-year-old pontiff wincing, clutching his face and rubbing his eye after the beads appeared to hit him as his vehicle slowed near the altar at Las Palmas Air Base.
Leo showed no obvious signs of injury and continued with the Mass, marking the end of his six-day visit to Peru and a grueling 12-day tour of South America , Reuters reported.
An estimated 1.5 million people attended the farewell Mass, where the pope thanked Peruvians for their hospitality and reaffirmed his deep connection to the country, which he considers his second homeland.
POPE LEO DRAWS STAGGERING 800,000 FAITHFUL TO HEART OF PARIS FOR MASSIVE OUTDOOR MASS
Leo showed no obvious signs of injury and continued with the Mass, marking the end of his six-day visit to Peru and a 12-day tour of South America. (REUTERS/Pilar Olivares)
"I wish to confirm you in faith and charity and assure you that I will always carry you with me. Yes, the Peruvian people are my people, too," he told the crowd.
The incident came as the pontiff traveled through crowds of faithful Catholics in his popemobile, a specially designed vehicle equipped with security features to protect the leader of the Roman Catholic Church .
Leo has previously been seen catching dolls, flags and other gifts tossed by worshipers as he travels in his popemobile.
During an appearance in St. Peter's Square, he even accepted pizza offered by fellow Chicagoans, according to Reuters .
At another event in Rome, the pope accidentally struck a Vatican cameraman riding behind him while reaching for a flying gift, prompting him to apologize to the operator.
HOW A CHICAGO BANK TELLER ONCE HUNG UP ON POPE LEO, WHO REPORTEDLY CALLED FROM THE VATICAN TO ADJUST NUMBER
Pope Leo XIV appeared to be struck near the eye by a rosary Monday as he reached out to catch prayer beads tossed toward his popemobile ahead of a farewell Mass in Lima, Peru. (REUTERS/Pilar Olivares)
Born Robert Prevost in Chicago in 1955, Leo became the first American pope in May 2025, when 133 cardinals gathered in the Sistine Chapel and elected him to lead the world's 1.4 billion Catholics.
Stepping onto the balcony of St. Peter's Basilica before thousands of cheering faithful, he had greeted the crowd with the words, "Peace be with you."
He also paid tribute to Peru at the time, since he spent decades serving as a missionary and bishop there before becoming pontiff.
POPE LEO XIV SEEN FOR FIRST TIME SINCE LUNG CANCER SURGERY AMID MAJOR RECOVERY MILESTONE
His tour began in Uruguay and went through Argentina before ending in Peru. (AP Photo/Andrew Medichini)
Switching to speaking in Spanish at the event on Monday, Leo told the crowd, "I would particularly like to say hello to my compatriots from Peru. It was a great pleasure for me to work in Peru."
Pope Leo's South American tour began in Uruguay and carried on through Argentina before ending in Peru.
The trip included 12 flights, two helicopter rides and nine Masses, as well as 36 speeches.

The trip came weeks after Leo underwent surgery to remove a lobe of his right lung.
Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

articles.title_orig: Three China-related Items to Consider as Trump Again Meets with Xi
articles.title_zh: Three China-related Items to Consider as Trump Again Meets with Xi
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
SEOUL — President Trump will get his wish for a historic meeting among the three most powerful men in the world — Xi Jinping of China, Vladimir Putin of Russia and himself — at a summit Thursday in southern China.
But Moscow, Beijing and Washington already know their leaders are arriving at the Shenzhen conference with disparate aims.
Trump hopes to focus the meeting on nuclear nonproliferation, urging the Russian and Chinese presidents to work with him to scale back the world’s largest nuclear stockpiles. Putin pressed for the meeting to discuss his ongoing war in Ukraine . And Xi wants to discuss neither, only embracing the idea of the summit to show the world China can help broker peace on the international stage, Chinese officials told The Times.
“That’ll be interesting,” Trump said earlier this week,  teasing the trilateral summit before the White House formally confirmed the meeting Friday.
“We’re talking a lot of things, including denuclearization,” he added, “but we’ll be talking a lot of things.”
U.S. officials have acknowledged they do not expect the meeting to result in a breakthrough on arms control. China is openly racing to build up its nuclear capacity — a nonnegotiable policy in Beijing, which sees its arsenal dwarfed by an American stockpile nearly 10 times the size.
“We do not expect to get to any kind of agreement. I would characterize this as the entry point,” one senior Trump administration official said. “This is the beginning of hopefully a conversation that can be productive going forward.”
Trump’s break from long-standing tradition in U.S.-Russia relations was real, but it should not have been entirely surprising.
The Chinese, too, threw cold water on the chances of a breakthrough, with one Chinese official telling The Times the central government saw no benefit to a pause.
“It is a matter of survival,” the official said.
The United States and Russia still command the world’s two dominant nuclear arsenals, with over 5,000 warheads each. China has an estimated 620 — but in catching up, it is developing new warheads with more sophisticated delivery systems.
Moscow, too, is modernizing its weapons, after the Trump administration allowed the last major U.S.-Russian nuclear arms treaty to expire earlier this year.
Though expectations are low for a nuclear breakthrough, Trump doesn’t want to discuss Putin’s priorities, either, the U.S. official added.
“He does not intend to talk about Ukraine in that meeting,” the official said. “China is not really part of that track, so it doesn’t really seem appropriate.”
Ukraine has grown increasingly concerned by Trump’s pressure campaign to force it into concessions to Moscow as he pushes to end the war.
The Trump administration has brought Russian and Ukrainian officials together at a working level to explore the viability of peace talks. But a long-standing U.S. policy on the war — not to negotiate about Ukraine without Ukraine — could be further compromised at a trilateral with Putin and Xi.
The only American business leader confirmed to join Trump in Asia is Elon Musk, the Tesla and SpaceX chief who was seen as instrumental in the decision last month to restrict Ukraine’s access on the battlefield to Starlink , the satellite internet service owned by Musk.
Beijing has struck a careful balance on Ukraine, publicly issuing its respect for sovereign borders — a position popular among Chinese voices who support Kyiv — while giving Moscow diplomatic cover, an economic lifeline and technological support throughout the war.
The summit’s stark lack of substance surprised even the closest China watchers.
Their competing agendas could make the summit little more than a spectacle, yet still produce images that hark back to the famous Yalta Conference — held in Crimea, the Ukrainian peninsula currently occupied by Russia, in 1945 — where Josef Stalin, Franklin Delano Roosevelt and Winston Churchill carved up a postwar order.
The summit on Chinese soil offers Xi a powerful image to broadcast worldwide , demonstrating an emergent superpower can bring together the leaders of two historic rivals in the name of peace.
Putin gets to present himself as a global player, despite the devastation wrought on Russia’s economy and military standing after four bruising years of war.
And it allows Trump to reassert his global relevance after this month’s midterms delivered the worst electoral rebuke to a president in half a century, rivaling the backlash against President Nixon during Watergate.

articles.title_orig: You can now assign Gemini ‘tasks’ for free in six countries
articles.title_zh: You can now assign Gemini ‘tasks’ for free in six countries
articles.content_orig:
Starting today, the Gemini app’s “tasks” feature, previously known as Spark, is now available for free users after requiring AI Pro in the past.
Google previously referred to this capability as a 24/7 personal agent before integrating directly into the main Gemini app experience in October . Above the prompt box on mobile (or below on the web), you’ll see “Chat” and “Task.” The first option is the existing chatbot, while the latter lets you “hand off even more tasks to Gemini.”
With tasks, Google’s “goal is for Gemini to save you time and money.” Google shared use cases like:
With today’s announcement, Google is emphasizing that “Gemini is your best choice as a personal assistant because [your emails, calendar, passwords, photos, files, and payment cards] already lives at Google securely, and you don’t have to send it elsewhere.”
Behind the scenes, Gemini tasks work in your own “hardware-isolated virtual machine” that’s sandboxed and has protections against prompt injection, while leveraging Google Safe Browsing when browsing the web.
Other safety features include having you confirm purchases and asking “clarifying questions if an instruction is ambiguous.”
Powered by the new Hydrogen model , free Gemini tasks are available in the US, Japan, Korea, Canada, Australia, and India.

articles.title_orig: FAA pauses installation of new routers after ground stop
articles.title_zh: FAA pauses installation of new routers after ground stop
articles.content_orig:
The Federal Aviation Administration said Tuesday it would pause the installation of new routers after problems with the technology led the agency to issue a rare nationwide ground stop on Friday.
Tens of thousands of flights were affected by the ground stop, which halted departing flights for more than four hours. It was the longest halt to U.S. flight departures since 9/11.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Sunday that an overloaded router installed in southern Arkansas as part of an upgrade to a system overseen by L3Harris Technologies appeared to overwhelm systems that feed radar and other data for air traffic control.
The Wall Street Journal first reported the news about the pause.
The FAA and Department of Transportation have said L3Harris was working to convert the communications network from copper wires to fiber optic.
Democratic members of the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science and Transportation this week asked the FAA and the Department of Transportation for clarity on what went wrong.
"Identifying the device that failed does not establish why it failed," the senators wrote in a statement. "Modernization cannot come at the expense of operational safety."
The agencies have said they are working to figure out the root cause of the issue and have reiterated that there is no indication of a cyberattack or outside threat.
The senators also asked for a briefing with the FAA, L3Harris and Juniper Networks, which is making the new devices, by Monday. They asked the companies to lay out why the operational systems lacked sufficient redundancy and answer other questions about what led to the outage.
CNBC has reached out to L3Harris and Juniper Networks for comment.
Duffy on Friday called for Congress to approve $50 billion in funding for upgrades to the aging U.S. air traffic control system, more than he has previously asked for. Democratic lawmakers pushed back on the request, citing unspent money from existing funding, which includes Congress' approval last year of $12.5 billion for airport and air traffic control improvements over five years.
Senate Commerce Chair Ted Cruz, R-Texas, said Tuesday that he thinks there will be support for air traffic control modernization, but that the allocation should be specifically for safety upgrades.
"I don't think the full $50 billion will be funded," he said. "Some of that is not safety related, but we just discussed there, and what I expressed is that the request needs to be focused on safety modernization."
Aging equipment and a shortage of air traffic controllers have for years angered airline executives, who have complained about the cost of resulting disruptions.
— CNBC's Phil LeBeau , Leslie Josephs and Justin Papp contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Putin's Crimean Bridge partly collapses as Zelensky hails 'unprecedented' attack by Ukraine
articles.title_zh: Putin's Crimean Bridge partly collapses as Zelensky hails 'unprecedented' attack by Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
Ukraine has severely damaged a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, in what President Volodymyr Zelensky says was an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making.
Images shared by Ukrainian officials show a section of the Crimean Bridge has collapsed into the water, dealing a logistical and symbolic blow to Moscow's war effort.
The Kremlin said it would rebuild the bridge "better than before" and that Russian President Vladimir Putin had been briefed on the overnight attack.
Elsewhere, Kyiv Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko said the Pivnichnyi (Northern) and Pivdennyi (Southern) bridges - key crossings over the Dnipro River - had been closed after Russia hit Ukraine's capital overnight.
The Southern bridge partially reopened on Tuesday, Klitschko said.
Ukraine has long targeted the Crimean Bridge, which provides a road and rail route for Russian soldiers heading towards the front line, but has struggled to close it for good.
While Kyiv has been trying to increase the cost to Russia of waging war economically, by hitting oil refineries and depots, striking the bridge is an attempt to increase the political cost on Russian President Vladimir Putin.
The timing of the strike comes at a significant moment, ahead of Putin meeting the leaders of China and the US. This could cloud his moment back in the spotlight.
The Crimean Bridge was built by Russia after it invaded and illegally annexed Ukraine's southern peninsula in 2014.
The $3.6bn (£2.7bn) piece of infrastructure is widely seen in Russia and Ukraine as Putin's personal pet project: His close tycoon friend Arkady Rotenberg built it, and then Putin personally opened it by driving a lorry over it in May 2018.
In Ukraine, the much-hated bridge is seen as one of the main symbols of Russia's continuing occupation of Ukrainian lands.
"We're drinking champagne!" Andrii, an engineer who lives in Kyiv, told the BBC.
He said the latest attack would "deal a very heavy blow to the morale of the Russians".
Some Ukrainians are concerned that Putin might now respond by carrying out even more attacks against civilian infrastructure, but Andrii said: "I don't think the Russians can make things much worse; they're already pounding us every single night with everything they've got."
The damage after the overnight attack, involving cruise missiles and drones, appeared to be far more severe than during previous strikes on the bridge, with a large arched section apparently destroyed.
Video footage appeared to show critical damage to the road section, with remnants of the support arch and road deck seen protruding from the water below.
Zelensky said the strike was the result of a seven-stage operation by the military and security services, which saw Ukrainian forces "gradually destroy air defence systems, radars, electronic warfare equipment, and other designated targets on the way to the final objective".
He said several types of Ukrainian drones as well as the country's Flamingo and Neptune cruise missiles were fired overnight during a "pivotal stage".
The Ukrainian president also said the rail section parallel to the bridge's road had also been hit by a wave of drones, though images showed its supporting arch was still standing and Russia's transport ministry later said some rail services resumed.
Ukraine's state security service SBU said its operations had "systematically suppressed enemy air defence systems" over a month, and said it showed "no Russian defence systems can guarantee the safety of illegal objects occupied by the invaders".
Meanwhile, Ukraine's military said the roadway on the bridge is "out of action", with no vehicle able to cross it, and the railway section is still standing, but with a damaged arch.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the bridge would "be restored following Ukrainian strikes, and it will be even better than before", and did not rule out the possibility the strikes were linked to Putin's visit to China.
Russia's Investigative Committee confirmed structural damage and said it had opened a "criminal case... on terrorism charges" after attacks by "Ukraine's armed formations".
For the second day in a row, Russia recorded the biggest Ukrainian drone attack since the war began, with 2,256 drones downed, according to the defence ministry.
Zelensky had warned of major attacks in the days leading up to a meeting between Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in China's Shenzhen on Thursday.
In Kyiv, loud explosions were heard just before midnight on Monday, with Klitschko saying shortly after that the city had suffered "damage to critical infrastructure systems" and disruption to heating and water supplies.
On Tuesday, Zelensky said four ballistic missiles had targeted the Southern Bridge, and another three had been fired on the Northern Bridge.
Some of Kyiv's above-ground metro services were also damaged in the overnight attacks, local officials said, after civilians were told to go to civil defence shelters.
Eight major bridges span the Dnipro River, connecting the western and eastern parts of Kyiv, and an estimated three million residents rely on the bridges to travel across the city.
Elsewhere, three people have been injured in a Russian missile attack in the central Cherkasy region, according to local officials.
The long-term impact of the Crimean Bridge strike is still not fully clear, though the risk of a serious transport and logistics crisis for the Russian military has increased significantly.
The collapse of the arched section has cut off the peninsula's direct road and rail links with Russia – at least until the crossing can be repaired.
However, there is still a land corridor running through the occupied parts of Ukraine's southern Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions - though Kyiv has been systematically striking transport routes across northern Crimea, as well as bridges and other crossings in the area around Chongar.
This has already caused problems with the delivery of fuel and other supplies, including military cargo.
There is a ferry crossing across the Kerch Strait, which connects the Black Sea with the Sea of Azov. It could partly compensate for the loss of the bridge, but its capacity is very limited and it is also vulnerable to attack.
Russia could also supply Crimea by sea, but this route is also risky, as Ukrainian naval and aerial drones operate extensively in the area.
In addition, debris from the Crimean Bridge – particularly its enormous arch – may have blocked the shipping channel.
This would make it harder for larger vessels to pass through and create further problems for the Russian-occupied ports in the Sea of Azov, including Mariupol and Berdyansk.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Approximately one-fifth of Ukraine is now under Russian occupation and Kyiv has refused Putin's demand to give up areas of Ukraine's eastern Donbas that remain under its control.
Additional reporting by Jaroslav Lukiv

articles.title_orig: A Kremlin trap? Europe sees danger in Vladimir Putin’s new demand in U.S. talks
articles.title_zh: A Kremlin trap? Europe sees danger in Vladimir Putin’s new demand in U.S. talks
articles.content_orig:
LONDON — When European nations said they wanted greater involvement in Ukraine peace talks , this was almost certainly not what they had in mind.
Europe has long demanded more say in negotiations to end Russia’s war , fearful of being frozen out by Washington and Moscow. They dread a deal favorable to President Vladimir Putin — who will meet President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping at a historic three-way meeting in Shenzhen, China, on Wednesday.
The good news for them is that the United States says it is now pushing to include Europe in the next rounds of diplomacy. The bad news, say governments, officials and foreign policy analysts, is the alarming new suggestion from Trump’s team: that the entire future of European security should be up for discussion too  — the same demand that Putin has pushed for years .
To the Russian leader, redrawing Europe’s security map means scaling back NATO’s presence, righting what he perceives as the injustices imposed on Moscow after the Soviet Union’s collapse. A succession of senior European officials have lambasted the idea, warning that Washington risks “walking into Moscow’s trap,” as Kaja Kallas, the European Union’s foreign policy chief, put it.
“This is all rather bizarre,” former Estonian President Toomas Hendrik Ilves said, summing up this sentiment in an interview with NBC News on Monday.
It’s not clear how or why the U.S. came to float a maximalist demand that Putin first made in 2021, one that was widely rejected by Western governments months before Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine . But in recent days, as Washington ups its pressure for a breakthrough in peace talks, Russia and the U.S. have both revived the idea.
Jared Kushner, the president’s son-in-law and envoy, wrote Friday that talks should tackle the “broader postwar European security arrangements.”
Earlier this month, he lamented “decades of mistrust” and “competing security concerns” between Russia and Europe, vowing to address these by building an “enduring framework for long-term European security and stability.” Kushner has also stressed that NATO would remain central to European defense and that no country should have a veto over another’s alliances.
Trump himself has also hinted that he seeks a final deal encompassing the entire continent. “It’s going to be a big agreement and it’s going to involve more than Ukraine,” he told reporters in the Oval Office earlier this month. “I could even say it might involve all of Europe. It’s going to be a big, beautiful agreement, and everyone’s going to be thrilled.”
Instead, the idea has been met with unease and dismay, viewed by many in Europe as echoing Putin’s hard-line war goals.
Whereas Kushner described Europe and Russia as neighbors unable to resolve their differences, the historical record shows the aggression has chiefly been directed one way. Russia seized Ukraine’s Crimean Peninsula in 2014, then launching a full-scale invasion in 2022, while waging sabotage, cyberattacks and disinformation against the West.
Kushner’s suggestion also touches on a central European fear: that Washington will pursue a deal at almost any cost, even if  that emboldens Putin to expand his aggression.
“Why are two real estate agents pushing this idea?” Ilves  said referring to Kushner and Steve Witkoff, another Trump envoy, both of whom made their fortunes in real estate before entering diplomacy.
“These people aren’t even diplomats,” said Ilves, who led his former Soviet republic from 2006 to 2016. “I’m not sure they have much of an idea of the long history of the development of security architecture in Europe relating to Russia.”
Asked about the criticisms, assistant White House press secretary Olivia Wales said the U.S. proposal sought to “strengthen existing European security arrangements, with NATO at their core, while developing practical mechanisms to prevent future conflict.”
Security guarantees for  Ukraine “cannot be designed without understanding the broader security framework in which they will operate,” she said in an email, adding that any final agreement must respect Europe and Ukraine’s sovereignty “and be agreed by the relevant parties.”
European officials are nonetheless unnerved by Kushner’s remarks.
Kallas, the E.U. foreign policy chief, described Russia’s maximalist war demands as “really absurd,” while German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul pointed out that “Europe has a security architecture — we don’t need a new one.”
Elsewhere, Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys said the rules were not the issue: “The problem is that Russia is breaking them.” And even Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney was adamant that the “security architecture for free Europe will be determined by free Europe and NATO, not by Russia.”
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described the idea as “dangerous,” saying that European security “should not be the main agenda.”
Ukraine’s view is that Russia is in no place to make such demands, given that it’s spent more than four years failing to win the war.
“At this stage, the most Putin can negotiate is a fair ceasefire along the current line of contact,” Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha said. And “frankly, Europe does not need a new security order; it already exists, and Russia is constantly violating it.”
Kyiv and its European backers also argue that a ceasefire must come before any peace talks, accusing Russia of stalling so it can keep bombing civilian infrastructure ahead of the frigid winter.
If Europe accepts Russia’s demands about wider continental security before there is a ceasefire, Moscow “will try to create the impression that it’s our fault that the war continues, because we don’t want to accept all their demands,” according to Sven Biscop, a director at the Egmont Institute, a Belgian think tank.
He said he believed dialogue with Russia is a good thing, a view echoed by influential Finnish President Alexander Stubb, who in an interview with the Financial Times published Tuesday said that it had been “irresponsible” to outsource talks with Putin to the U.S., which he said could be leaning toward carving up Europe into spheres of influence.
Back in Washington, the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, D-N.H., urged Trump’s team to refuse Putin’s demands.
The Russian leader not only wanted control of Ukraine but “he wants to redesign NATO to accommodate his revisionist ambitions,” Shaheen said, adding that any discussions about European security infrastructure should be a “nonstarter,” for the U.S. which “has benefited from the Alliance.”
Amid all of this, any substantial progress toward ending the war remains elusive.
The latest round of talks between the U.S., Russia and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, last week produced no major breakthrough. Kushner said Washington was working toward what could be the largest prisoner swap of the war, while reporting that Russia had agreed to give Europe a seat at the table during the next round.
Russia hasn’t quite confirmed that, instead saying that it needs “to understand from the Europeans themselves” what they can “contribute to the peace process” before allowing them to join, as Putin’s spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters Monday.
There has been some internal wrangling among the European nations about who might represent them. Leaders have agreed on a team comprising the United Kingdom (which left the E.U. in 2020), France, Germany, Italy and Poland, alongside representatives of the European Commission and European Council. Kallas herself was left off the team.
“I don’t know who among the current leaders could be a sane dialogue partner,” Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov told the state-run news agency Tass on Monday.
He likened the chosen group of European countries to “the Quartet,” a satirical poem by Russian author Ivan Krylov. In it, a monkey, a donkey, a goat and a bear blame their failure to form a string

articles.title_orig: Google makes it easier to use Gemini without training AI on your data
articles.title_zh: Google makes it easier to use Gemini without training AI on your data
articles.content_orig:
It can be hard to use Google products—or even the Internet itself—without coming into contact with Gemini AI. That is, of course, by design . The more you use Gemini, the more data Google collects to train and improve its generative AI chatbot. The options to limit training on your data have been scant, but Google is finally adding more controls to the Gemini app.
The change currently rolling out to Gemini will separate your chat history from training, which allows you to retain basic AI functionality without handing Google quite so much control over your data. Prior to this change, the only way to opt out of contributing your chat contents (including attachments) for training was to turn off your history. That made it impossible to go back and pick up a chat down the road.
As the new settings roll out, users will see separate toggles for model training and chat history. The history setting will continue to support an adjustable limit, but you will no longer have to change it to stop Google from training on your Gemini usage. Meanwhile, AI training will be an opt-out situation. You’ll need to find the toggle to block Google from using your chats for AI training. It’s under Activity in the Gemini settings. You can also access the menu from your Google account under Data and Privacy > My Activity > Other activity > Gemini Apps Activity.
Importantly, this only applies to future interactions with Gemini. If you have previously fed any data into Google’s AI, that’s already part of the training data. That can include your inputs, Gemini’s responses, uploaded files, tool calls, your location, and data from connected apps. Google says it may retain this data for up to three years to improve its models. The company has previously noted it attempts to filter personal information out of the Gemini activity history, but that isn’t a guarantee.
Regardless of your chosen activity settings, you can always manually remove anything you don’t want saved on the same page with the history and training toggles. However, reviewed chats that are already part of the training data won’t be retroactively deleted. Opting out of training doesn’t mean Google won’t have your data, either. Google may use this data in other ways for up to three years—it just won’t add it to AI-training data sets.
If you want to use Gemini and not retain any data, your options are actually a bit more limited now. Currently, if you disable history, Google still retains that data for 72 hours (and 24 hours for the user). Once the updated page is live, this duration will change to two months. So you can access that data for longer, but so can Google. The company says this is to “respond to you, process your feedback, and protect Google, its users, and the public.” Essentially, Google will be more able to identify nefarious AI usage even if someone disables history.
Even with the longer chat retention, the ability to control AI training is still a welcome privacy improvement. Google says the change is rolling out globally, but it may take a few weeks to show up for everyone.

articles.title_orig: Trump’s New A.I. Chip Rules Rattle Southeast Asia
articles.title_zh: Trump’s New A.I. Chip Rules Rattle Southeast Asia
articles.content_orig:
The Trump administration’s proposal to restrict China’s access to advanced A.I. chips overseas rattled Southeast Asia on Tuesday, threatening a data center investment boom fueled by Chinese companies using the region to sidestep U.S. restrictions on Nvidia’s most powerful chips.
Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand and Singapore have become offshore computing hubs for Chinese companies such as Alibaba and ByteDance. Data center operators in those countries provide the Chinese firms with remote access to advanced Nvidia chips they cannot buy directly or bring into China.
The strategy has drawn billions of dollars in investment to the region. But in Washington, officials seeking tighter controls on China’s A.I. sector have increasingly viewed data centers as a workaround that poses economic and national security risks.
Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, was ousted last week after revelations he had an affair with a woman who formed a Singaporean data center company called Megaspeed. U.S. authorities deemed the woman, Alice Huang, to be an asset for Chinese intelligence services, and they are investigating Megaspeed over allegations of smuggling chips to China. China has denied that Ms. Huang was spying for it.
Separately, Nvidia’s board of directors announced on Tuesday that it had established a committee to oversee “the company’s national security policies, export control compliance and global trade risk management.” Nvidia’s board is engaged in a search for a permanent successor to Mr. Huang. The company’s interim chief executive, Colette Kress , is set to preside over the release of the company’s latest quarterly financial results later on Tuesday.
Shares of technology companies tumbled on Tuesday. In trading in Hong Kong, Alibaba fell more than 5 percent, while Tencent’s stock dropped nearly 4 percent. The Chinese A.I. firms MiniMax Group fell more than 7 percent and Z.AI declined more than 5 percent. In the United States, tech stocks slid lower, pulling the Nasdaq index down more than 1 percent. Nvidia shares faced choppy trading ahead of its earnings results, which are expected after the market closes.
