articles.title_orig: Dow falls 700 points as tech shares decline, traders monitor NSA network outage: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Dow falls 700 points as tech shares decline, traders monitor NSA network outage: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
Stocks dropped on Tuesday, pressured by renewed selling in semiconductor names, as traders braced for Nvidia's much-anticipated earnings report.
Reports of a a National Security Agency network outage added to recent jitters about the stability of the country's technology infrastructure and helped weigh on the market, traders said.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 866 points, or 1.7%. The Nasdaq Composite lost 1%, while the S&P 500 slipped 1.3%. The Dow was down more than 920 points at its session low.
Major averages fell to their lows of the day following the report from CNN that said a classified network used by the spy agency had gone down, citing six people familiar with the matter. CNN's sources said there was no evidence that it was a cyberattack.
The NSA later in the day put out a statement saying the agency "experienced temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance." The agency added that "mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational."
Traders said the report helped take equities lower, though the losses were contained. This outage is latest in a string of incidents that have left people on edge including the FAA ground stop over the weekend, Microsoft's Outlook outage last week and some recent issues with banking apps.
Nvidia shares trades off their lows of the session after former CEO Jensen Huang said he would be open to returning as CEO if the company's board thought that was in the best interest of shareholders. Traders are on edge ahead of the chipmaker's earnings after the bell.
"Nvidia should report strong results and guidance, but [it] is unlikely to be able to give investors solid answers to the questions heavily weighing on the stock [regarding] leadership and investigations around export controls," Ross Mayfield, investment strategist at Baird, told CNBC. "Strong demand might stabilize things, but the next leg higher will need some clarification around the 2028 and beyond outlook."
Despite Nvidia's share comeback, the rest of technology was lower with Micron Technology sliding roughly 6%. Advanced Micro Devices slipped more than 1.5%, while Intel was down 4% and Marvell Technology shed more than 2%.
Microsoft shares were down 3% and among the biggest tech lowers.
Neocloud stocks CoreWeave and Iren shed 5% and 6%, respectively. Nebius lost 4.2%. Investor Steve Eisman told CNBC earlier in the day that these stocks had the most to lose if the Huang scandal causes Nvidia to pull back its financing of the AI ecosystem.
A CNN report Tuesday that a classified network used by the National Security Agency is down was just the latest to hit a stock market that's been battered lately by negative headlines. These include the FAA ground stop over the weekend, as well as Microsoft's Outlook outage last week.
"Any one of the stories that have have broken over the course of the last week or so would be enough to cause the market jitters. But when you compound that by having multiple stories — whether it's today's NSA report or the FAA ground halt or Microsoft Outlook being down for two days or Chase Bank ATMs not working — aggregate all of those, and it's easy for the human mind to get to a place where there must be something larger at play here," said Art Hogan, chief market strategist at B. Riley Wealth. "What's causing the market to have the kind of drawdowns that it's having today, it's just that aggregate of the compounding of bizarre stories that just have become too much of a headwind, at least in the near term," he added.
Investors may not be moved by Nvidia's upcoming earnings results, according to Megan Horneman, chief investment officer at Verdence Capital Advisors.
"I don't think there's going to be anything surprising from the earnings report," she told CNBC. "I don't know that we're even going to get much forward-looking information that people may be trying to get information on."
Horneman expects uncertainty to persist for the technology sector as investors assess what the trade could look like after "parts of Nvidia start to unwind."
"We're just stuck in this, I think, panic type of stage right now, and I don't know how far it will go," she said.
Another strong round of economic data, particularly on the consumer side, has led Goldman Sachs to take up its growth forecast.
The firm now sees  fourth quarter gross domestic product accelerating by a 2.4% annualized pace, up 0.6 percentage point from its prior outlook. Moreover, Goldman raised its backward-looking expectation for the third quarter, now looking for 3.8% growth from the period, which would be 0.4 percentage point higher than the advance estimate from the Commerce Department.
At the core of the more optimistic outlook is a retail sales report Tuesday that showed receipts up 0.2% in October — 0.6% when excluding autos and when focusing on the components that feed directly to GDP.
"The strength of today's report continues to reflect the resilience of the US consumer this year, as boosts from tax refunds and positive wealth effects from equity market gains have more than offset the drag from higher energy prices," Goldman chief economist Jan Hatzius said in a note.
Selling was broad across Wall Street midday Tuesday as declining stocks outnumbered advancers by nearly 3 to 1 on both the New York Stock Exchange and Nasdaq.
Declining volume accounted for roughly 69% of total NYSE volume and 71% on the Nasdaq, according to FactSet data.
On the NYSE, 1,924 stocks declined while only 700 rose. For Nasdaq, decliners totaled 3,036, compared with 1,141 advancers.
New lows also outpaced new highs. The NYSE recorded 362 new lows against just 20 new highs, while the Nasdaq logged 679 new lows versus 38 new highs.
— Deena Zaidi and Scott Schnipper
A recent CNN report that the National Security Agency's classified communications network has gone down dragged the major averages to their lows.
At its session low, the Dow Industrials were down 922.66 points on the day, while the S&P 500 shed 1.7%.
CNN, which cited six people familiar with the matter in its story, said that there is no evidence of a cyberattack.  The New York Times also confirmed the report, noting that the network is used to transmit top secret information.
This development is unfolding on the heels of recent tech disruptions, including the  Federal Aviation Administration's ground stop last week and the massive Microsoft outage .
Wall Street is feeling good about Disney after the company reported a beat on revenue and earnings-per-share for its fiscal fourth quarter, reported on Tuesday. Five pieces of equity research scanned by CNBC all had buy, outperform or overweight ratings on the stock.
JPMorgan had some concerns about changes in Disney's reporting methodology on streaming video, and Goldman Sachs flagged cord-cutting as a key downside risk among other factors, per notes from Nov. 16 and 17.
Steven Cahall at Wells Fargo has an overweight rating and a price target of $132, per a Nov. 17 note.

The boutique investment bank said in a note dated Monday that the after-tax value of Berkshire's equity portfolio increased by about $1.2 billion from the start of this quarter through Nov. 16.
This comes after the Omaha-based conglomerate raised its stake in Delta Air Lines in the third quarter while reducing its stake in Bank of America .

articles.title_orig: Trump is heading to China for APEC amid renewed calls to curb Nvidia chip sales. Here's what to watch
articles.title_zh: Trump is heading to China for APEC amid renewed calls to curb Nvidia chip sales. Here's what to watch
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia warned its customers that new legislation on Chinese companies remotely accessing its artificial-intelligence chips could expose it and them to U.S. "legal action," sources told CNBC.
The chip giant is facing increasing scrutiny from U.S. lawmakers over Chinese companies' access to its advanced chips, which U.S. export controls restrict from going to China.
Nvidia messaged chip buyers in recent months to caution that the proposed Remote Access Security Act, or RASA, would give the U.S. government broader authority to control access to cloud services in the same way as physical hardware, potentially exposing both parties to legal risk, according to two people with direct knowledge of the matter. The people asked not to be named while discussing private communications.
It also said that, for now, it would not sell its chips to customers who rent more than 50% of the graphics processing units, or GPUs, to Chinese companies, the people said.
Separately, the Financial Times reported earlier this month that Nvidia verbally told data-center clients to direct at least 51% of their services to non-Chinese customers under future contracts.
Regulators have had limited powers to control companies' access to those chips through cloud services hosted overseas.
RASA passed the House of Representatives in January but has not yet passed the Senate. Remote access to the chips has provoked the ire of President Donald Trump 's administration, which has sought to keep the chips out of China to maintain the U.S. lead in the AI race.
CNBC reported on Nov. 5 that Chinese lab Moonshot AI sought access to Nvidia chips through data centers in Europe. The Trump administration previously singled the company out, accusing it in July of accessing the chips through centers in East Asia.
The U.S. Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS, announced on Monday an interim final rule designed to prevent Chinese companies' remote access to AI chips.
Nvidia and BIS did not respond to a request for comment.
On Sunday, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called for a "dramatic shakeup" at Nvidia after Jensen Huang 's shock departure as CEO, amid reports of an extramarital affair with a woman U.S. authorities reportedly suspect of spying for China.
Bessent suggested other Nvidia executives should face scrutiny over the chip giant's compliance with export controls.
"I want to keep coming back to what was the culture at Nvidia, and were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?" Bessent told Fox News.
In an August securities filing , Nvidia said it sought to "strictly comply with all applicable export control regulators" but did not have "physical control of our products after sale" and relied on its customers' and partners' compliance programs.
Huang has been asked to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 3.

articles.title_orig: Hacker Who Leaked Grand Theft Auto VI Clips Pleads Guilty to Cybercrimes
articles.title_zh: Hacker Who Leaked Grand Theft Auto VI Clips Pleads Guilty to Cybercrimes
articles.content_orig:
A hacker responsible for high-profile cyberattacks, including stealing footage from Grand Theft Auto VI in the hope of blackmailing its publisher, pleaded guilty to several crimes, British prosecutors said.
Arion Kurtaj, 21, pleaded guilty to cybercrimes including illegally impairing computer systems, as well as to fraud, Britain’s Crown Prosecution Service said in a news release on Monday.
“His offending was calculated,” said Robert Hutchinson, a prosecutor, adding that even after being charged, Mr. Kurtaj continued to break the law.
He will be sentenced on Monday in a London court, prosecutors said. Mr. Kurtaj’s publication in 2022 of footage illustrating the gameplay of Grand Theft Auto VI, a closely guarded sequel 13 years in the making, sent shock waves through the industry.
The recent guilty plea was another turn in a long case against Mr. Kurtaj, who was found unfit to stand trial before that finding was reversed.
Prosecutors said he was a member of a hacking group, Lapsus$, and that he had launched attacks on several companies while he was still a teenager.

articles.title_orig: Take-Two’s Firaxis, Maker of ‘Civilization,’ Cuts a Third of Its Staff
articles.title_zh: Take-Two’s Firaxis, Maker of ‘Civilization,’ Cuts a Third of Its Staff
articles.content_orig:
The Civilization and XCOM developer is shrinking as a new XCOM game has missed a development milestone, according to Bloomberg
Take-Two Interactive $TTWO 's Firaxis Games cut roughly 60 jobs on Tuesday, about one-third of the studio's workforce, according to Bloomberg .
A spokesperson from 2K Games, the Take-Two imprint that oversees Firaxis, verified that Heather Hazen, who heads the studio, is departing, according to Bloomberg. The Maryland-based studio makes the Civilization and XCOM franchises.
"Firaxis is restructuring and recentering around the studio's core strength — designing world class strategy games that have set the industry standard for the genre for the last 30 years," the spokesperson said in a statement, according to Bloomberg. "As part of these changes, the size of the studio is being reduced to focus on design, technology and the player experience, which means saying goodbye to talented colleagues who helped build Firaxis."
The spokesperson described Hazen’s exit as a planned handover, according to Game Developer . “With the studio entering this reset, she feels this is the right, deliberate moment to hand over the reins to ensure the next studio leader has full ownership of this new era from the start,” the spokesperson said, according to Game Developer.
Firaxis has been working on a new XCOM title that ran into development problems and fell short of an important milestone this summer, according to Bloomberg. Bloomberg, citing unnamed people, said work on the game will go on, though the cuts could bring major changes to it.
“Civilization VII,” the studio’s latest title, came out last year to a lukewarm response and has been patched repeatedly since, according to Bloomberg. The game holds a 51% positive user rating on Steam, according to Kotaku .
The layoffs land just two days prior to “Grand Theft Auto VI” hitting the market, according to Bloomberg. Rockstar, a separate Take-Two label, develops and publishes that game.

articles.title_orig: 6-year-old girl dies in gene-editing trial, leading to scientist's firing, Chinese state media reports
articles.title_zh: 6-year-old girl dies in gene-editing trial, leading to scientist's firing, Chinese state media reports
articles.content_orig:
A Chinese scientist who concealed the death of a 6-year-old girl in a gene-editing trial has been fired following a government probe, according to state media.
The girl died last year after receiving experimental gene therapy to correct a non-life-threatening condition — which was not disclosed in published research, an investigation found in July.
Neuroscientist Zilong Qiu, the trial's lead researcher, had made no mention of the girl in a paper published in the prestigious journal Nature, according to the joint investigation by Science and Retraction Watch .
"According to official documents and accounts provided by the girl's parents, the hospital had allowed Qiu's experimental treatment to proceed under a regulatory provision that does not require approval from national regulators," Science reported in July. "After the child's death, the hospital paid a modest fine to a local health authority but Qiu was not publicly sanctioned."
Qiu was dismissed as deputy director of the Songjiang Research Institute affiliated with Shanghai Jiao Tong University, state broadcaster CCTV said Friday, citing a statement from Shanghai authorities.
The reported statement included only Qiu's surname, but referenced the Nature study published on Feb. 18.
Qiu was given a five-year suspension from participating in scientific projects and recorded in a database for "serious breaches of research integrity," the report said.
Another researcher on Qiu's team was fired and handed a five-year suspension, while several others with ties to the hospital where the trial took place were also punished.
The child who died had a rare neurodevelopmental condition called Snijders Blok-Campeau syndrome, according to the report.
The hospital's ethics committee had approved a gene-editing trial to treat the disorder in January 2025, the report said.
The committee terminated the study after the girl died in March due to complications from gene therapy.
Shanghai authorities found that Qiu's team failed to properly inform the hospital of possible safety issues from earlier tests on primates, according to the report.
AFP has reached out to Qiu for comment.
The July investigation by Science and Retraction Watch found that the girl's parents, who paid more than $800,000 to fund the experiment, were not adequately informed about the risks.
"Learning the reality of these missing safeguards has fundamentally changed how we now view the entire project," the girl's father, told Science . "We did not realize how unusual and dangerous many of the arrangements were."
The scandal is a blow to China's ambitions to rival the United States as a biotech power following the 2018 scandal around He Jiankui , a biophysicist who secretly produced gene-edited babies. He was later sentenced to three years in prison.

articles.title_orig: Cash Hidden in Forests? Hungary Goes After Corruption Under Orban
articles.title_zh: Cash Hidden in Forests? Hungary Goes After Corruption Under Orban
articles.content_orig:
Hungary’s new anti-corruption agency made an eye-catching splash last week when it released photographs of a table piled with bank notes worth nearly $20 million. The money, the agency said, had been found hidden in forests and farm buildings during a hunt for funds stolen during the long tenure of the country’s former prime minister, Viktor Orban.
This week, Hungary’s new leader, Peter Magyar, announced that the stacks of cash photographed by the National Asset Recovery and Protection Office, a new agency set up as part of what he calls “operation cleansing fire,” were just the “tip of the iceberg.”
To display the full volume of money ransacked by corrupt officials before Mr. Orban lost a general election in April , Mr. Magyar told Parliament on Monday, “You would have to put 10,000 tables next to each other.”
In his telling, the total amounts to more than 60 trillion Hungarian forint (more than $180 billion) — a staggering, and so far unproven, sum in a small Eastern European country whose total spending on defense last year was around only $5 billion.
While Mr. Magyar is prone to exaggeration by character and political calculus, his angry denunciations of Orban-era corruption resonate with many Hungarians and helped his party win the April election.
Mr. Orban and his die-hard supporters have dismissed the photographs of recovered cash and a rash of detentions as hollow political theater aimed at discrediting and destroying opposition to Mr. Magyar, who was sworn in as prime minister in May.

articles.title_orig: Federal Reserve's Cook refuses to participate in White House hearing - ABC News
articles.title_zh: Federal Reserve's Cook refuses to participate in White House hearing - ABC News
articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook declined through her lawyers to appear next month before a Trump administration committee that is considering whether she should be fired, calling the process unfair and committed to a predetermined outcome
WASHINGTON -- Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook declined through her lawyers to appear next month before a Trump administration committee that is considering whether she should be fired, calling the process unfair and committed to a predetermined outcome.
The refusal extends the wrangling between the White House and Cook's lawyers regarding her appearance before the committee, which the administration initially demanded for Nov. 6 . Trump administration officials have demanded that Cook appear before the committee to address allegations she committed mortgage fraud in 2021, before she joined the Fed's board of governors, a charge she denies.
President Donald Trump has sought to fire Cook since August 2025, and she has argued that the president's efforts to do so represent a threat to the Fed's independence and reflect Trump's desire to force the central bank to reduce borrowing costs.
“Governor Cook has no legal obligation to participate in an unfair hearing — and indeed, has a duty to the Federal Reserve to decline to participate in any proceeding that would undermine the institution’s unique status and independence,” Abbe David Lowell, Cook's lawyer, wrote in a letter released Tuesday to White House counsel William Scharf. The three-person panel set up by the White House to consider the allegations “appears to be a façade designed to obscure a predetermined decision to fire Governor Cook.”
In June, the Supreme Court blocked the Trump from removing Cook while litigation over the attempted firing continues, finding that "the fact of independence but also the appearance of independence is key to the Federal Reserve’s design.”
Trump officials have threatened to move ahead with the hearing even without Cook, and in a Nov. 3 letter said that the three-member committee “reserves the right to draw adverse inferences against you” for not participating.
The unusual “committee of inquiry” set up by the White House consists of Kevin Hassett, Trump’s top economic adviser; Andrea Lucas, whom Trump appointed to lead the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission; and Keith Sonderling, Trump’s pick for Labor Secretary.
The Supreme Court said in a footnote to its June ruling that Trump could try again to fire her if the administration provided her adequate notice and an opportunity to respond. The committee of inquiry is an effort to meet those conditions.
Under the law governing the Fed, the president can only fire a Fed governor “for cause,” but the Supreme Court didn’t address whether Cook’s actions met that standard. The committee will ultimately recommend whether there is cause to fire Cook, the White House has said.
Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh was asked at a press conference Oct. 28 if he or the Fed would be involved in the hearing against Cook, and he said, “not to my knowledge.”

articles.title_orig: Facing Criticism, Trump Administration Says It’s Investigating Megaspeed
articles.title_zh: Facing Criticism, Trump Administration Says It’s Investigating Megaspeed
articles.content_orig:
The Justice and Commerce Departments announced late Monday that they were pursuing a criminal investigation of Megaspeed, a Singapore company once led by a woman whom U.S. officials believe worked as a Chinese intelligence asset while having an affair with Nvidia’s chief executive.
The announcement appeared to be an effort to counter criticism that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick was slow to investigate Megaspeed. It has become the most prominent example of companies that American authorities believe are skirting export rules on the powerful artificial intelligence chips made by Nvidia, the world’s leading manufacturer.
Nvidia exports have exposed a rift in the Trump administration between officials who believe American A.I. technology needs to be kept out of China for national security reasons and others who want a more hands-off approach to export controls.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a TV interview on Friday that his department had been pushing for months to add Megaspeed to a trade blacklist, but that the Commerce Department “holds the pen.”
“You will have to ask them about their internal processes,” he said.
That the Justice Department was included in the Monday night announcement appeared to add heft to the investigation’s importance and signaled to critics that administration officials did not intend to ignore the issue.
Megaspeed was created and led for a time by Alice Huang, who U.S. officials say was an asset for Chinese intelligence. The New York Times reported last year that she and Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, had a close relationship, and last week Mr. Huang admitted that he had been unfaithful to his wife with Ms. Huang.

articles.title_orig: Iran targets US sites in Bahrain after 2-month pause
articles.title_zh: Iran targets US sites in Bahrain after 2-month pause
articles.content_orig:
Gulf states have been worried for weeks that Iran may again begin to target them in an effort to force a resolution to the nine-month regional conflict on its terms.
In the past few days, that anxiety has deepened with two attempted drone attacks on Bahrain, an American ally that hosts major US military facilities, while Tehran has also warned the Gulf states not to “reopen old wounds.”
Iran appears to be raising the stakes as it struggles to prevent more Gulf oil and gas from getting through the Strait of Hormuz as its economy labors under US blockade and the cumulative effect of international sanctions.
The Bahrain Defense Force said Sunday it had “intercepted and destroyed” several Iranian drones, after a similar interception on Friday.
The US Embassy in Bahrain on Sunday urged Americans to exercise “heightened vigilance,” citing an increased threat of attacks by Iran-backed Houthis and Iranian efforts to target US government officials and facilities in the region. The embassy also warned of possible flight cancellations, airspace closures and other travel disruptions, while noting that it remained open.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) had earlier claimed an attack on a US helicopter base in Bahrain, saying it was in retaliation for unspecified US “aggression.” CNN has reached out to US Central Command for comment.
The targeting of Bahrain has been accompanied by a more belligerent tone out of Tehran toward Iran’s neighbors, the consequences of renewed US or Israeli strikes and the state of negotiations with the US.
Iran was incensed by suggestions from the six-member Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) last week that it would have to pay its neighbors compensation for attacks on their territory, something Iran itself is seeking in any deal with the US.
“How can countries that actively participated in military aggression against a neighboring country and made their airspace, territory and waters available to those who attacked Iranian territory speak of seeking compensation from Iran?” asked Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei in a news conference on Sunday.
“What about Iran’s inherent and legal right to defend itself?”
In a reminder that Iran does not forget the past, Baghaei said the Gulf states “must be careful not to reopen old wounds,” referring to their support for Iraqi dictator Saddam Hussein in the war with Iran in the 1980s.
Iran wants the Gulf states “to pay the price for a war they did not choose, then give up their right to accountability and compensation. This is an equation that cannot be accepted,” said Ebtesam Al-Ketbi, of the Emirates Policy Center think tank, on Sunday.
A sign of growing unease about the prospect of renewed hostilities came last week when the GCC announced an advanced headquarters in Kuwait for its unified military command and the deployment of forces to the facility.
The organization’s secretary general, Jasem Mohamed Al Budaiwi, said the move showed “a firm Gulf commitment to safeguarding the security and sovereignty of the GCC states” following what he called “heinous Iranian attacks.”
Iran has also stepped up attacks on shipping in the Gulf, with almost daily claims – few of them substantiated – that tankers have struck mines as they’ve tried to transit the Strait of Hormuz.
For Tehran, the increase in Gulf energy exports to close to pre-war levels in recent weeks, and the sharp decline in oil prices, deprive it of vital leverage in negotiations. The International Energy Agency said Gulf oil exports - excluding Oman - reached 18.4 million barrels a day in October, about 26% below prewar levels.
At the same time, Iran has been unable to export any meaningful amount of its own crude for more than two months.
The Iranian regime is demanding an end to the US blockade, the progressive removal of international sanctions and an unfreezing of billions of dollars in frozen assets as conditions for resuming negotiations with the US.
But US President Donald Trump appears content to let the economic squeeze on Iran take its course, anticipating that Tehran will have to soften its terms and recognizing the Gulf states want to avoid another round of conflict.
“At the request of the nations that I am ⁠looking to protect, we are doing it a little bit longer way, a bit more civilly,” Trump said Thursday. At the same time, he canceled efforts by Vice President JD Vance to resurrect talks with Iran, declaring: “We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed.”
Indeed, Iran’s economic pain appears to be deepening even as senior officials in Tehran insist it can withstand the pressure and can access hard currency to support the rial, whose value has fallen drastically since the conflict began.
One perpetual sign of hardship is the long lines seen at gas stations in many parts of Iran.
Esmail Saghab Esfahani, a vice president, acknowledged last week that there was a supply problem and that Iranians could no longer count on fuel stations to meet their needs.
Some residents of the port city of Bandar Abbas blocked traffic on Thursday to protest against fuel shortages. The speaker of the Iranian parliament, Mohammed Bagher Ghalibaf, suggested officials stop talking about the fuel issue, always sensitive in Iran.
And yet there are no public indications the regime is ready to compromise.
Baghaei was asked Sunday whether Iran would accept a temporary suspension of uranium enrichment or a reduction in enrichment levels in negotiations with Washington.
“No. We are not at that stage at all. During this period, we are not discussing any details related to the nuclear issue, nor have we held any such discussions.”
Ghalibaf said Sunday it made no difference whether Washington wanted negotiations or war.
“If the Americans make another mistake this time, the capabilities and will of Iran’s armed forces will determine the geography of the battlefield.”
Iran has frequently warned that another chapter in the conflict will see it broaden targets to infrastructure across the region, including subsea cables.
Additionally, its Houthi allies in Yemen fire ballistic missiles at Saudi Arabia almost daily and appear to have put Saudi-backed government forces under renewed pressure in the south of Yemen, forcing them to retreat from near the Red Sea in a setback in their campaign.
The result is an unstable limbo across the region.
“The United States may believe it can maintain the blockade for an extended period, but Iran sees it as a direct threat to its economy, sovereignty, and national security,” Israeli analyst Danny Citrinowicz, a senior fellow at the Institute for National Security Studies, wrote on X.
The US “cannot assume that time alone will force Tehran to surrender. Iran has repeatedly demonstrated its willingness to absorb enormous economic costs rather than abandon what its leadership considers fundamental national interests.”

articles.title_orig: Trump talks Nvidia, rare earths as he attends Quad and Asean meetings in Manila
articles.title_zh: Trump talks Nvidia, rare earths as he attends Quad and Asean meetings in Manila
articles.content_orig:
David E. Sanger and Katie Rogers
President Trump landed in Manila on Tuesday to begin a 48-hour Asia trip in which he will meet with Xi Jinping of China and other world leaders, with an unpredictable agenda that could include the future of American tariffs, nuclear arms control, the war in Ukraine and U.S. restrictions on advanced A.I. chips.
Mr. Trump was scheduled to meet with President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. of the Philippines and attend a gathering of Southeast Asian leaders. After less than 24 hours in Manila, he will head to the APEC economic summit in Shenzhen, China, where he was expected to meet with Mr. Xi and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia.
The brief itinerary appears to reflect Mr. Trump’s preferences. He dislikes big summits where he often is not the sole subject of attention. And he enjoys meeting with leaders of powerful nations — especially Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin, two authoritarian leaders he often talks about in admiring terms.
Mr. Trump will be meeting Mr. Xi for the third time this year, and a three-way meeting between China, Russia and the United States would be the first of its kind.
On Tuesday, Mr. Trump caught the end of a dayslong meeting of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, or ASEAN, after issuing tariffs on countries across the region, even allies. Those moves added to a sentiment in Asia that the United States was not a reliable partner but rather one that treasured its commercial interests over its security interests. The only event of substance on the president’s schedule on Tuesday — signing what he had called a “ trade deal ” with Thailand — did not happen because Mr. Trump said it was still being finalized.
Mr. Trump met with leaders from the so-called Quad — the United States, India, Japan and Australia — soon after his arrival. All three partners are smarting from high energy prices triggered by the Iran war, a conflict Mr. Trump never discussed with them before launching it in late February.
In Shenzhen — the heart of China’s robotics and artificial intelligence industries — Mr. Trump will pursue détente with Mr. Xi. He needs to extend a soon-expiring trade truce that limited tariffs on Chinese goods entering the United States in return for a Chinese commitment not to cut off rare earths and magnets.
Then comes the main event: the meeting with Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin. Referring to the trilateral meeting, Mr. Trump told reporters before leaving Washington: “We are going to be talking about denuclearization, a tough subject because it is very hard for any of us to say we’ll get rid of our nukes.” Chinese officials have made clear they are not interested in nuclear talks until their arsenal is roughly the size of the American one.
Mr. Trump also said, “We will talk about Iran a little,” insisting the situation was in “very good shape.” Analysts say it is unlikely that the meeting will make any progress on Iran, with Russia happy to see energy prices elevated since the war began, and China eager to see them rapidly decline.
Here’s what else we’re covering:
Protests: Thousands of demonstrators assembled in downtown Manila on Tuesday in opposition to Mr. Trump’s visit and to a U.S.-led initiative called Pax Silica, which aims to unite partners around A.I. supply chains independent of China. Read more ›
North Korea: Mr. Putin could meet with Kim Jong-un if the North Korean leader also travels to China for the APEC summit, Russian state news agencies reported, citing the Kremlin’s spokesman. It was not clear whether Mr. Kim would attend the summit.
Ukraine: Mr. Trump also said he would talk about Ukraine, on which Mr. Putin’s aides are engaging in talks with the U.S. and Ukrainian officials, but also renewing demands that NATO pull back its troops to where they were before the alliance expanded toward Russia.
President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia could meet with Kim Jong-un if the North Korean leader travels to China for the APEC summit this week, the Kremlin said, reflecting the deepening of ties between their countries in recent years.
Asked about the possibility of a meeting, Dmitri S. Peskov, the Kremlin spokesman, said on Monday that it would “of course” happen if Mr. Kim went to Shenzhen, the Chinese economic hub and host city, according to Russian state news agencies. North Korea has not confirmed whether Mr. Kim plans to attend the summit.
Mr. Putin and Mr. Kim have publicly met three times since 2022, and North Korea has been a key supporter of Russia’s military actions in Ukraine.
As the war in Ukraine nears its fifth anniversary, with no end in sight, the Kremlin is expected to use Mr. Putin’s many meetings at the APEC summit to showcase how Russia is regarded as one of the major international powers alongside the United States and China.
A visit by Mr. Kim would be a rare foray outside North Korea for the leader, and it would further raise the prospect that he could meet with President Trump in China. On the first day of his 48-hour trip to Asia, Mr. Trump told reporters that Mr. Kim “would like” to come to the APEC summit. The president has repeatedly said he would like to meet with Mr. Kim again.
On Wednesday, Mr. Putin is scheduled to meet with Xi Jinping, China’s leader. On Thursday, he is set to take part in a trilateral summit with Mr. Xi and Mr. Trump, the first meeting of its kind. The Kremlin said on Monday that it was working to arrange a bilateral meeting between Mr. Putin and Mr. Trump.
Before his departure for China, Mr. Putin met on Monday in the Kremlin with Jo Yong-won, a secretary of North Korea’s ruling Workers’ Party. During the meeting, Mr. Putin said that North Korea’s help in driving Ukrainian forces from the Kursk region of Russia last year “marked a new chapter in the history of military cooperation between our countries.”
Moscow planned to unveil a monument in Kursk by the end of the year to honor the North Korean troops, Mr. Putin said.
During the final meeting of the day, with ASEAN leaders, President Trump told President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. of the Philippines: “I don’t want to date myself, but I knew your parents very well. They were great. I believe in genetics. They did a good job. You have very good genetics, I can tell you that.”
It was not the first time Mr. Trump has praised the family of Mr. Marcos , who is the son of the dictator Ferdinand E. Marcos, who ruled the Philippines for 20 years, imposed martial law and was ousted in 1986.
The only event of substance on President Trump’s schedule today, the signing of a trade deal between the United States and Thailand, did not happen because it was still being finalized. Trump told reporters that “Thailand will eliminate all tariffs on U.S. imports” and that the United States would provide tariff relief, but the two sides signed only a memorandum about the agreement. The president said the deal would be done in the coming weeks.
During an address to Quad leaders, President Trump called Prime Minister Narendra Modi of India, which is a member of the group, “a great leader and a friend of mine, highly respected by everybody all over the world.” The president also praised Modi as he stood with other leaders and took a few questions, calling him a “very tough man.”
India and the United States are navigating a rocky patch in their relationship, largely tied to trade and India’s purchases of Russian oil. Although Modi and Trump signed an interim framework for a trade deal in February, talks have dragged on, frustrating both parties.
The Nvidia turmoil and its implications for the U.S.-China relationship is a backdrop to President Trump’s visit. On Tuesday, shares of technology companies in Asia tumbled after the Trump administration announced rules to restrict overseas access to advanced A.I. chips like those sold by Nvidia. In Hong Kong trading, Alibaba fell 5 percent, while Tencent’s stock dropped nearly 4 percent. The Chinese A.I. firms MiniMax Group fell 7 percent, and Z.AI Co. declined 5 percent.

articles.title_orig: Customers report outages at Chase, Bank of America and Wells Fargo
articles.title_zh: Customers report outages at Chase, Bank of America and Wells Fargo
articles.content_orig:
Thousands of Chase Bank customers reported they had trouble using their online accounts on Monday.
“JPMorganChase has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug,” a spokesperson said Monday. “It is taking longer than usual to service some customers.”
The Chase spokesperson went on to say it was a “bug,” rather than a widespread cyberattack.
Social media users reported issues with transactions at physical Chase branches, as well, and some local bank branches told customers earlier in the day that they were having issues with their internal system. However, Chase said in a statement that “customers still have access to their accounts and funds.”
The outage wasn’t caused by a cloud-related issue or a cyber attack, a source familiar with the matter told CNN. Rather, an update on the company’s own physical computer systems inadvertently caused issues.
As of 2:00 p.m. ET, more than 4,700 customers reported issues with Chase, according to Downdetector.
Customers reported issues at other major banks, including Bank of America, Wells Fargo, and U.S. Bank, though on a smaller scale.
The reports with the other banks appear to be related to sending money through Zelle, a digital payment network, to Chase accounts.
“U.S. Bank systems are not directly impacted. However, clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays,” U.S. Bank said in a statement.
Bank of America also said it was operating normally on Monday.
“Clients experiencing delays with other providers may wish to contact them directly for the latest information,” a spokesperson told CNN.
Zelle said that its service is “operating as it should.” The money-transferring service is owned by a consortium of US banks called Early Warning Services, and Zelle said it does not hold consumer funds.
“An issue at the financial institutions may be impacting broader services, including Zelle payments, for some of their customers,” a Zelle spokesperson said.
Chase also said it wasn’t a systemic issue.
“Other banks may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us,” the spokesperson continued.
Monday’s Chase outage marked the third straight weekday with a massive technical failure.
On Thursday, a Microsoft outage cut off email access to millions of people across 74 countries and territories. On Friday, a Federal Aviation Administration systems failure led to a nationwide ground stop .
And on Monday afternoon, United Airlines reported a systemwide computer problem that delayed flights.
The incidents don’t share the same scope or root causes. Microsoft blamed a Windows defect, a traffic overload and capacity constraints. The FAA cited a router deployment issue and excessive data flooding its systems. It’s not yet clear what caused the Chase or United outages on Monday.
But the glitches share a common theme: “the complexity and fragility of the systems that we depend on every day,” Mike Chapple, a professor of IT, Analytics, and Operations at the University of Notre Dame, said in emailed comments.
“In each of these cases, what started as an issue in one small part of a larger system quickly spread, causing massive disruptions nationwide,” he added.
Complexity and interdependence aren’t inherently flaws — in fact, they make systems more resilient, noted Rebecca Krauthamer, CEO and cofounder of QuSecure, a cryptography provider for the US government.
“But when dependencies on systems aren’t sufficiently understood, failures can cascade across institutions and industries,” she added.
Think about it like the Titanic: The watertight bulkheads were unable to withstand a failure that exceeded the ship’s architects’ worst-case-scenario assumptions. Even the best-designed systems sometimes succumb to threats and problems that the designers couldn’t have imagined when they built them.
The problem with interdependent technology systems is that system failures are rarely isolated incidents: Our heavy reliance on a handful of systems means failures have tended to bring down systems across the world.
“The question for leaders is not whether one system will fail but how many other things fail with it, and how fast you can contain it,” said Madhu Shashanka, founder of Concentric AI.
This story has been updated with additional developments.
CNN’s David Goldman contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Tracking China’s War of Words Against Japan
articles.title_zh: Tracking China’s War of Words Against Japan
articles.content_orig:
A headline in the Global Times, a newspaper controlled by China’s ruling Communist Party, about Japan’s “remilitarization” after China restricted exports to Japanese entities. Credit... Andy Wong/Associated Press
By Javier C. Hernández and Gal Koplewitz
Javier C. Hernández reported from Tokyo, and Gal Koplewitz from London.
When China’s leader, Xi Jinping, met with President Trump at the White House earlier this fall, the two leaders toasted to friendly relations.
But in private, Mr. Xi offered Mr. Trump a stark warning about Japan, a U.S. ally, according to two officials briefed on the talks, who requested anonymity to discuss private conversations. Mr. Xi told Mr. Trump that Japan’s recent military buildup threatened to destabilize Asia, the officials said, and that Mr. Trump should be cautious about working with Japan’s prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, describing her as a “militarist.”
The warning from Mr. Xi was part of a broader effort by China to isolate and undermine Japan after Ms. Takaichi said last year that Japan could be forced to defend Taiwan in case of a Chinese invasion. China considers Taiwan, a self-governed democracy that lies just 69 miles from Japan’s westernmost island, part of its territory.
Since the comments, Mr. Xi has overseen a campaign involving propaganda and diplomacy to target Japan, according to interviews with officials and scholars, and an analysis by The New York Times of Chinese Foreign Ministry briefings and state media. It is all part of a push, analysts say, to persuade the world that Japan is a resurgent aggressor.
China has deployed words and images to portray Japan as a World War II-era enemy, using phrases like “remilitarization” and “neo-militarism,” and videos that compare Japan to a “rampaging gray rhino.”
Chinese officials have repeatedly sought to belittle Ms. Takaichi, Japan’s first female prime minister, omitting her title in official briefings, breaking with longstanding practice. State media has depicted Ms. Takaichi in short skirts and a nurse’s uniform in cartoons, and described her as “Abe’s girl,” referring to Shinzo Abe, the former Japanese prime minister and Ms. Takaichi’s mentor.
In private conversations with Western scholars, Chinese academics have recently pushed the narrative that Japan is the “Israel of East Asia,” poised to lead the United States into conflict and destabilize the region.
Russia has helped amplify China’s talking points, branding Japan as a threat. Moscow has echoed Beijing in describing Japan as an “ enemy state ” that is not to be trusted, invoking a World War II-era designation used against former Axis powers.
Mr. Xi and Ms. Takaichi will cross paths this week at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit meeting in Shenzhen, China. The encounter is expected to be frosty; Mr. Xi might try to use the summit as an opportunity to alienate Ms. Takaichi from Japan’s allies, experts say.

articles.title_orig: 'Inside Deutsche Bank': The secret documents linking Trump to dirty Azerbaijani money
articles.title_zh: 'Inside Deutsche Bank': The secret documents linking Trump to dirty Azerbaijani money
articles.content_orig:
Deutsche Bank’s headquarters in Frankfurt. The bank long resisted breaking with Russia’s most important business titans under President Vladimir V. Putin. Credit... Felix Schmitt for The New York Times
By Russ Buettner Khadija Sharife Brian Fitzpatrick Frederik Obermaier Bastian Obermayer and Sophia Baumann
When Russian missiles began pummeling Ukraine in February 2022, executives at one of the world’s largest banks sensed trouble headed their way.
Within hours of an invasion that set off a war that is now in its fifth year, Western governments issued new financial sanctions intended to further isolate Russia from the world economy.
At Deutsche Bank, a longtime bank of Russian industry titans and oligarchs, officials scrambled to get ahead of the damage. “Russian Sanctions Urgent Request” read the subject line of an email sent by one of Deutsche’s anti-financial crime specialists to her colleagues.
“As you know we have a large Russian Oligarchs client population” and other clients with investments in Russian companies, she wrote. She asked which of those clients “we potentially could unwind and which not.” Should the bank advise them, she wondered, to withdraw their money “while they still can?”
This email exchange was the beginning of a frenzied reckoning within the scandal-plagued bank over its long resistance to breaking with Russia’s most important business titans under Vladimir V. Putin, the Russian president. The bank’s clients included the Russian billionaires Oleg V. Deripaska and Viktor F. Vekselberg. Time and again over many years, records show, Deutsche Bank’s risk managers warned that such relationships were perilous.
But profits associated with maintaining its Russian clients won out every time.
Russia’s war in Ukraine swept up Deutsche Bank in a larger shift. For decades, German politicians and business leaders believed that working with Russia and deepening economic ties between the two countries would discourage Russian aggression. That strategy collapsed after the invasion.

articles.title_orig: Homebuilder sentiment plunges to 14-year low, leading more builders to drop prices
articles.title_zh: Homebuilder sentiment plunges to 14-year low, leading more builders to drop prices
articles.content_orig:
Sentiment among U.S. homebuilders dropped to the lowest level in 14 years, as higher mortgage rates, higher costs for energy, materials and labor, as well as weaker consumer confidence, led to more builders cutting prices.
Builder confidence in the single-family housing market fell four points to 25, according to the National Association of Home Builders/Wells Fargo Housing Market Index, or HMI. That is the lowest since April 2012, when the market was just recovering from the housing crash and foreclosure crisis. Last November, the index stood at 38.
Mortgage rates pulled back slightly in October, but surged higher again last week. The average rate on the 30-year fixed hit 7.51% on Monday, according to Mortgage News Daily. Last year at this time it was 6.38%.
Of the HMI's three components, the index measuring current sales conditions fell six points to 28, and future sales expectations dropped two points to 30. Buyer traffic declined two points to 16 — its lowest level in 15 years, excluding the start of the pandemic in 2020.
"Builders are confronting multiple challenges in today's economy," Bill Owens, NAHB chairman and a home builder and remodeler from Worthington, Ohio, said in a release. "Stepped-up immigration enforcement is keeping legal workers off job sites, deepening labor shortages and driving up costs. Higher fuel prices are prompting subcontractors to raise their rates sharply, and with fewer buyers in the market, more builders are scaling back construction."
More builders are now cutting prices as they try to get buyers in the door. In November, 46% of them  reduced prices, the highest share in the post-Covid period, according to the report. The share of builders using sales incentives also hit a post-Covid high of 68%. That was the 20th consecutive month in which at least 60% of builders used them.
"The housing market faces a range of supply-side challenges,  including building material costs pushed higher by tariffs, an ongoing shortage of construction workers and excessive regulations that undermine housing affordability," Robert Dietz, NAHB's chief economist, said in the release. "Mortgage rates above 7%, softer consumer confidence and an uncertain economic outlook are holding buyers back."
In the three-month moving averages for regional HMI scores, the Northeast dropped four points to 34, the Midwest fell five points to 35, the South fell three points to 27, and the West posted a three-point decline to 23.

Get unlimited access to everything VICE has to offer.
With Grand Theft Auto VI now just 24 hours away from launch, players who are waiting to see what critics think have one big question: when do reviews come out? Here is everything known so far about the supposed GTA 6 review embargo date.
At the time of writing, Rockstar has not confirmed a GTA 6 review embargo date. In fact, the studio hasn’t even publicly announced anything about reviews. While rumors about potential dates have floated online, all of it is purely speculative and does not have an official source.
However, it should be pointed out that Grand Theft Auto VI officially launches early November 18 morning in New Zealand time. So the game will technically have launched by that point, which might give us an indicator of when first impressions of the game could eventually go up from players in that region.
So to sum it up, there is no GTA review embargo date currently known or announced .
Recently, Bloomberg announced that Jason Schreier will host a live GTA 6 Q&A on Wednesday, November 18 at 8 a.m. PT / 11 a.m. ET . The outlet invited fans to ask Schreier “anything about Rockstar’s blockbuster video game.”
The timing led some fans to wonder whether Schreier had already played GTA 6 and whether reviews might be live by the time the Q&A starts. That said, Bloomberg’s announcement doesn’t say whether Schreier has played the game or whether the outlet plans to publish a review, so that part is still speculation.

It should also be pointed out that Schreier has visited Rockstar North previously to preview Grand Theft Auto VI . The veteran journalist did a pretty extensive deep dive into the development of the game. So the Q&A could be in reference tot hat.
According to Rockstar’s release schedule , GTA 6 unlocks at midnight local time on November 19 in each store region. When it hits midnight in Auckland, it’ll still be 3 a.m. PT / 6 a.m. ET on Wednesday, November 18 in the US.
That means that Rockstar fans waiting for first impressions of Grand Theft Auto VI should get them as early as November 18 at 6am PT once players in New Zealand have already made their way through the opening hours of the game. It also means that spoilers may start appearing online, so make sure to avoid them!

articles.title_orig: Anthropic Said to Guide IPO Price to Top of Range or Above
articles.title_zh: Anthropic Said to Guide IPO Price to Top of Range or Above
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic is likely to price its IPO above the current range of $70 to $78, multiple sources told CNBC's David Faber on Tuesday.
The artificial intelligence company is planning to close the order books and lock in total demand at 4 p.m. ET on Tuesday, according to the people, who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to speak publicly. Anthropic is slated to list on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol "ANT" and start trading on Nov. 19.
If Anthropic's IPO proceeds as planned, the company will debut roughly five months after SpaceX went public in a record offering that raised $85.7 billion. But Anthropic is facing a public market that's grown increasingly skeptical of the AI trade, as well as mounting and widespread antipathy toward the technology in the U.S.
A group of researchers, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei , co-founded the company in 2021 after defecting from OpenAI , now its chief rival. Anthropic is best known for developing a family of AI models called Claude , and it underwent a period of explosive growth in 2026, driven largely by the popularity of its AI coding tool, Claude Code .
For the nine months ended Sept. 30, Anthropic said it generated $33.24 billion in revenue, up roughly 1,200% from the same period last year, according to its prospectus . It reported a $104 billion net loss during the nine-month period, though most of that was due to the change in fair value of convertible notes and derivative liabilities. Anthropic lost $25.1 billion over the same stretch in 2025, the filing said.
Anthropic has long worked to establish a reputation as a safety-conscious AI company, and its prospectus included more than 90 pages of risk factors for investors to consider ahead of its listing.
"I think if we do this right, we can create an age of miracles where humanity is able to solve problems that have eluded us for millennia," Amodei said in Anthropic's roadshow video . "We have to make sure that all the risks, all the ways that things can go wrong with this technology, we very carefully address those risks as we bring the benefits and as we have a viable business at the same time."
"I invite you to join us on the next phase of this journey," Amodei said.

articles.title_orig: ‘A Possible Stampede’—Fed Issues Serious Bank Run Warning As Outages Fuel Wild November 17 ‘Blackout’ Theories
articles.title_zh: ‘A Possible Stampede’—Fed Issues Serious Bank Run Warning As Outages Fuel Wild November 17 ‘Blackout’ Theories
articles.content_orig:
By PHILLIP NIETO, US POLITICAL REPORTER
Published: 09:27 EST, 17 November 2026 | Updated: 14:17 EST, 17 November 2026
JD Vance has told Americans they do not need a bunker or a food stockpile, days after a global email collapse, a nationwide ground stop and a banking meltdown.
‘A lot of my friends have reached out asking if they should prepare to build a bunker or stock up on food and water,’ the vice president told Fox News host Laura Ingraham on Monday night.
‘We don’t see a crisis coming down,’ Vance added, ‘but you have to be prepared for everything.’
‘We want to make sure we prevent the worst outcomes, but we’re also prepared for the worst outcomes,’ he continued.
Ingraham had asked him point blank whether Americans should be prepping for a major global catastrophe. It comes after Britain and France have told their own citizens to keep days of food and water at home.
Vance brushed off the reporting behind the question, including accounts of Pentagon bases preparing to run off the grid for 90 days, as ‘just basic good government, making sure that our military is prepared, God forbid, if there was a crisis.’
Meanwhile, Google has warned corporate America that hackers powered by artificial intelligence are running autonomous attacks across major systems.
The company's report released on Monday claims these AI hackers can constantly work around security patches, write working exploits and fire them at online servers.
Vance has told Americans they do not need a bunker or a food stockpile, days after a global email collapse, a nationwide ground stop and a banking meltdown
Google has warned corporate America that hackers powered by artificial intelligence are now running autonomous attacks across major systems
Tens of thousands of travelers were left stranded over the weekend after the FAA issued a nationwide grounding for all flights
Google drew no connection between its findings and last week’s failures, and federal officials say they have found no evidence that anyone attacked anything.
Moreover, Hackers have compromised some of the world’s most visited websites in a sweeping cyberattack targeting users’ money and credit card details.
Security researchers identified malicious code in website tools used by 178 organizations, including Zoom, CNN, the BBC, HSBC, Equifax, Salesforce, Peacock, IKEA, Fox News, NPR, the ASPCA and Invisalign.
The attack, detected Monday evening, targeted Optimizely, a service companies use to test different website layouts and features.
Microsoft’s Outlook, Teams and Copilot services collapsed on Thursday and stayed down for users in 74 countries into the weekend.
On Friday, approxiatemately 10,000 flights were disrupted after the Federal Aviation Administration halted departures across the country, the second nationwide ground stop since the September 11 attacks.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has blamed a router that contractor L3Harris Technologies installed at a remote FAA radio site in Arkansas.
It flooded a network still running on equipment built in 2001 and scheduled for replacement in 2006.
Duffy called FBI Director Kash Patel to pull agents into the investigation, the router now sits in a laboratory in Florida, and the FAA has switched off the broadcast function on all 69 of the same devices across the national airspace.
By Monday, banks had been affected by the the outages as thousands of customers at Chase, Wells Fargo, US Bank, Capital One, Truist and Bank of America reporting they could not see their balances or move cash.
United Airlines also delayed its own departures that same afternoon when pilots lost the weight and balance figures they need to leave the gate, stopping hundreds of flights.

articles.title_orig: Elon in, Jensen out: Trump leans on Musk during latest China visit
articles.title_zh: Elon in, Jensen out: Trump leans on Musk during latest China visit
articles.content_orig:
The president is headed this week to summits in the Philippines and China that will include a meeting with Xi Jinping and a trilateral meeting with Xi and Vladimir Putin.
President Donald Trump heads to China later this week for talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping on trade and denuclearization, but one topic that won’t be on Trump’s agenda, according to U.S. officials, is Nvidia.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation after an extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy has sent political shock waves through Washington. Trump confirmed that the FBI was looking into the case, and lawmakers are demanding answers about whether China was able to access Nvidia’s advanced computer chips, which are used for artificial intelligence.
Leaving the White House Monday morning, the president said “I don’t know that she’s a Chinese spy” as he downplayed national security concerns. “It was not put at risk, and our country is now stronger than ever before. And you know, China plays games with us, and we play games with China. But our country now militarily is stronger than we’ve ever been,” Trump told reporters. The president also said he “wouldn’t mind” if Huang was reinstated as Nvidia CEO, but added he may talk to Xi about the spying allegations.
Still, despite the growing number of questions about Nvidia, a U.S. official who previewed the president’s trip to reporters in a background call Friday said it “should not really have any bearing on the trip in all of our discussions and negotiations with the Chinese.”
“I think when it comes to some of these national security matters and examinations and investigations that are going on in the U.S., it’s probably not something that we’re going to read the Chinese in on at this moment,” the U.S. official said.
Those questions about China’s access to advanced computer chips spilled out into the public last week. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent pointed the finger at Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick for not implementing stricter controls on exports of Nvidia chips to Megaspeed International, a company run by the alleged Chinese spy. Beijing has denied the espionage allegations.
The White House has expressed “complete confidence” in Lutnick, and a Department of Commerce spokesperson told MS NOW, “Secretary Lutnick has proactively agreed to appear voluntarily before the Banking Committee to address their questions.”
“These are national security matters that we develop in the administration,” the U.S. official said on the call, adding that it was an “interagency process” and that officials “don’t expect it to figure at all in any of our conversations with the Chinese while we’re there.” The official did say the U.S. was discussing closing “loopholes” in existing measures to control exports of advanced AI chips to China.
The president’s trip to Asia includes two international summits: first in Manila, Philippines, to meet with leaders of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, followed by Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meetings in Shenzhen, China. Accompanying the president, according to the White House are Bessent, Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, White House chief of staff Stephen Miller, National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett and U.S. Trade representative Jamieson Greer.
Last week Trump called Huang’s resignation a “horrible thing” and said he didn’t plan to raise the situation with the Chinese leader. But the president added, “I’m sure President Xi will ask me about it. I just know Jensen very well. I just think he’s a very honorable man. I mean, he built a great company.”
In May, Huang accompanied Trump on a trip to China for a state visit. It was on that trip that Rubio briefed Trump about Huang’s alleged connection to a suspected Chinese spy, according to a U.S. official granted anonymity to discuss sensitive intelligence information. Trump has denied that he received that warning, which was first reported by The New York Times.
A second U.S. official on Friday’s preview call told reporters that SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk was expected to accompany Trump to Asia. The U.S. official said that Musk would be traveling as an adviser given his “tremendous business interests” in the U.S.-China relationship and that he was a “big part of our national security.”
One area Trump is expected to confront Xi over is China’s growing nuclear arsenal.
Previewing a trilateral meeting between Trump, Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin, a second U.S. official briefing reporters on the same call said it was time for China to “step up” to the “adult table” on nuclear nonproliferation talks. While Russia and the U.S. have larger stockpiles, the official criticized China’s rapid nuclear development, adding that “things that China is doing very opaquely with their nuclear arsenals” affect the “security of every human being in the world.”
The official added that the administration was not expecting any immediate denuclearization agreement from the trilateral meeting, stressing that the occasion would serve as the “entry point” for further efforts to reduce the number of nuclear weapons.
The three leaders are also expected to discuss the war with Iran, according to the U.S. official. Both China and Russia have provided an economic lifeline to Iran through their existing trade relationships, but Trump has downplayed any significant military support to Tehran.
There are no plans for a bilateral meeting between Trump and Putin at the APEC summit. The U.S. official said the president did not plan to discuss the war in Ukraine in the trilateral meeting given separate ongoing negotiations being led by Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. Musk, whose Starlink system has been used in the war by Ukraine, will not attend the trilateral meeting, the U.S. official said.
Trump told reporters Monday he may also meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. The president didn’t offer any additional information other than a potential meeting would take place in China.
After visiting Beijing in May, this will be Trump’s second trip to China this year, and his third meeting with Xi in as much time. Two months ago the Chinese president visited Trump at the White House. The trilateral will be Trump’s second official meeting with the Russian president in his second term, after an Alaska summit last year.
One contentious topic the Trump administration didn’t mention in its readout from the president’s last meeting with Xi is Taiwan. Chinese officials previewing APEC and Trump’s visit stressed to MS NOW in a mid-October press briefing that they continued to oppose Taiwan’s “independence” and U.S. arms sales to Taiwan.

articles.title_orig: How new US chip restrictions on South East Asia will hit China
articles.title_zh: How new US chip restrictions on South East Asia will hit China
articles.content_orig:
As US President Donald Trump heads to China, his administration has renewed efforts to curb Beijing's access to advanced semiconductors.
On Monday, Washington announced new interim rules that will increase scrutiny of  data centre operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil.
The move not only restricts the export of advanced chips, but also access to their computing power, which Chinese firms currently rent abroad to train artificial intelligence (AI) models.
South East Asian countries in particular have invested heavily in data centres to power their AI ambitions - and Chinese firms seeking computing power overseas have been a key market.
But now these firms will need a US government licence to buy advanced chips from Nvidia or other American chipmakers. This allows Washington to monitor if those chips are being used to serve Chinese companies, or being smuggled to China.
This poses a fresh challenge for Beijing, which has become deeply dependent on compute from abroad in the wake of US export restrictions. At least 30% of China's advanced AI computing power is projected to come from renting overseas or smuggling in 2027, according to research by the Institute for Progress , a US-based think-tank.
China's foreign ministry called the new rules "economic coercion" and said Beijing "will take necessary measures to firmly safeguard its own legitimate rights and interests".
This is also a problem for South East Asian economies where large numbers of data centres have sprung up recently. Some of the firms behind them are accused of helping China evade US export controls on advanced chips.
One of those is Singaporean data centre firm Megaspeed, whose former director Alice Huang is suspected of being a Chinese spy. Calls for tighter export controls have grown after Nvidia's Jensen Huang admited to an affair with her and resigned as CEO .
Megaspeed, the biggest buyer of Nvidia's chips in South East Asia, is accused of illegally smuggling chips to Chinese companies after purchasing them for use in data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.
The company has denied these allegations, defended its business as "legitimate and lawful", and said it has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation". It also said Alice Huang stepped down from her role as director in late 2023 and left the firm last year.
The US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, however, has said Brazil and the four South East Asian nations "present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion" of the chips that Washington wants to keep out of China's hands.
The new measures are aimed at ensuring sensitive US technology "cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries," the bureau added. Licences will be issued on a "case-by-case basis", it said.
Countries like Malaysia and Thailand whose data centre roll out has been heavily driven by Chinese buyers could be hit hardest, says international trade expert Naoise McDonagh from Australia's Edith Cowan University.
But the new rules are unlikely to derail the data centre boom as a whole, says Reema Bhattacharya from advisory firm Verisk Maplecroft, adding that investment backed by major tech firms and clearly identifiable customers should "remain relatively resilient".
Singapore was an early adopter of data centres but when it began limiting new construction, investment flowed to neighbours Malaysia and Thailand. Johor in Malaysia and Batam in Indonesia have also approved billions of dollars worth of data centres to catch the spillover demand.
These countries have been offering incentives such as cheaper land to attract foreign investment, including from Chinese tech giants Alibaba and Tencent.
But now, the region could find it harder to get hold of advanced chips.
The BBC has contacted Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand for comment.
Singapore said it is "engaging relevant US authorities" to understand the new rules better, and is "exploring how to facilitate trusted access" for local firms.
A spokesperson for Brazil's Ministry of Development, Industry, Trade and Services said it is aware of the US announcement and it "is closely monitoring any potential developments regarding this measure".
Malaysia previously said it welcomes data centre investment but "will not allow itself to be used to get around export controls".
The new rules also come just ahead of Trump's meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Shenzhen this week.
Beijing has made self-sufficiency in tech a national priority and needs the best chips to build powerful AI models.
Chinese firms DeepSeek and MoonShot have come close to US rivals like Anthropic and OpenAI. So much so that The Institute for Progress estimates top US AI models lead the best Chinese platforms by only about six and half months.
"This is despite US AI companies having significantly better compute access and financing," it said.
Still, China needs advanced US chips to ensure its best AI models are competitive, experts tell the BBC.
The new restrictions on South East Asia and Brazil have taken away "one of the more practical routes Chinese AI developers had to accessing frontier computing power," Bhattacharya said.
But tighter restrictions could also push Chinese firms towards domestic semiconductors and further drive advancement at home.
That has been a longstanding dilemma for Washington, McDonagh said: whether to keep selling chips to China to retain its reliance on the US, or restrict access and risk further spurring Chinese innovation.
